In both cases, the nonlinear manifold is constructed from an initial linear compression followed by an input-informed identification of the latent coordinates as general linear combinations of the retained modal amplitudes, incorporating graph information when relevant to seek the intrinsic dimensionality of the solution manifold. We show that combining the nonlinear-manifold representation with MAW-ECM reduces the number of sampled integration points by more than two orders of magnitude relative to the corresponding standard linear reduced model. Relative to the fixed-weight manifold models alone, the adaptive weights eliminate approximately 80% of the remaining points in the homogenization benchmark and more than 97% in the damage benchmark, while essentially preserving their accuracy.
tldr: A manifold-adaptive-weight empirical cubature method (MAW-ECM) is proposed for hyperreduction of nonlinear finite element models, achieving orders-of-magnitude reduction in sampled integration points while preserving accuracy.
motivation: Fixed-weight hyperreduction methods leave potential untapped; allowing weights to vary with latent coordinates can further reduce sampled spatial entities and improve computational efficiency.
method: The method builds on a fixed-weight ECM rule and greedily removes sampled entities via convex quadratic weight-redistribution problems with positivity constraints. Nonlinear manifolds are constructed from initial linear compression and input-informed latent coordinates.
result: On homogenization and damage benchmarks, MAW-ECM reduces sampled integration points by over two orders of magnitude versus standard linear reduced models, and eliminates ~80% (homogenization) and >97% (damage) of remaining points compared to fixed-weight manifold models with essentially preserved accuracy.
conclusion: Manifold-adaptive weights substantially enhance hyperreduction in nonlinear finite element analysis, enabling significant computational savings without sacrificing model fidelity.

title: Discrete Gromov-Wasserstein Duality: Algorithms And Isomorphism Testing
authors: Gabriel Rioux, Joanna Marks, Riccardo Passeggeri, Ziv Goldfeld
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance provides a principled framework for aligning metric measure (mm) spaces based solely on their intrinsic structure. Its ability to identify isomorphic representations of distributions across spaces renders it valuable for comparing data where equality up to isomorphism occurs naturally such as in graphs or, more generally, distributions on graphs. Recently, a type of dual form for the GW distance between Euclidean distributions with the squared Euclidean or inner product costs was derived, spurring the development of new statistical and algorithmic results for this setting. This work furnishes a novel duality result for GW distances with and without entropic regularization that is applicable to all finitely supported mm spaces. Leveraging this result, we derive the sample complexity of empirical GW distances between finite mm spaces, as well as limit distributions under proper centering and scaling. Furthermore, we propose new algorithms for solving the regularized GW problem which are subject to formal convergence guarantees. These statistical and algorithmic advancements give rise to a principled and efficient framework for testing whether two distributions on the set of graphs with a fixed number of nodes are isomorphic based on samples.
tldr: The paper introduces a new duality result for discrete Gromov-Wasserstein distances and applies it to develop statistical tools and algorithms for testing isomorphism of distributions on graphs.
motivation: To compare metric measure spaces and graphs based on their intrinsic structure, addressing the need for efficient algorithms and statistical guarantees in applications such as graph isomorphism testing.
method: Derives a dual formulation for discrete Gromov-Wasserstein distances, with and without entropic regularization, and uses it to establish sample complexity bounds, limit distributions, and new optimization algorithms with formal convergence guarantees.
result: Provides a principled framework for testing whether two distributions on graphs with a fixed number of nodes are isomorphic, backed by theoretical guarantees.
conclusion: Advances the theory and applications of Gromov-Wasserstein distances, offering both statistical and algorithmic contributions for structured data comparison.

title: Gradient-Free Optimization For Matrix Functions
authors: Sawyer Allen, Cash Cherry, Aidan Eck, Stephen Becker, Daniel Mckenzie
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the task of optimizing smooth, possibly non-convex functions of a matrix variable given access only to directional derivatives rather than full gradients. This setting arises when fine-tuning large neural networks on consumer-grade hardware: the network's weights are matrices, memory constraints rule out backward-mode automatic differentiation, but directional derivatives remain available through forward mode. We frame gradient estimation in this setting as a structured recovery problem, in the spirit of signal processing. From this perspective we provide three contributions. First, we introduce an alternative to the standard random gradient estimator; the difference corresponds to replacing the adjoint of the sampling operator with its pseudoinverse. Second, when the gradient satisfies an approximate low-rank condition, techniques from matrix sensing yield a family of highly accurate gradient estimators that drop into any first-order method. Third, we note that while the computational cost of such estimators is high, this can be amortized by combining them with a matrix-aware optimizer such as spectral descent. Specifically, the gradient estimator computes a factorization of the gradient, allowing for the projection step of spectral descent to be done at no extra cost. We demonstrate our findings with two careful numerical experiments on synthetic functions with approximately low-rank gradients. We show that by exploiting this low-rank property one obtains much faster convergence to good approximate solutions.
tldr: This paper proposes gradient-free optimization methods for matrix functions using directional derivatives and low-rank matrix recovery to enable fine-tuning of large neural networks on consumer hardware.
motivation: Fine-tuning large neural networks on consumer hardware is challenging due to memory constraints that prohibit full gradient computation, while directional derivatives are still accessible via forward-mode differentiation.
method: The authors frame gradient estimation as a structured recovery problem, introduce an alternative to random gradient estimators using pseudoinverse, and leverage low-rank matrix sensing for accurate gradient estimation, combined with a matrix-aware optimizer like spectral descent.
result: Numerical experiments on synthetic functions with approximately low-rank gradients demonstrate that exploiting low-rank structure yields faster convergence to good approximate solutions.
conclusion: The proposed estimators efficiently estimate gradients in memory-constrained settings, potentially enabling practical fine-tuning of large models on limited hardware.

title: G-Exponential Families Through Probability Coordinates
authors: Manuela-Simona Cojocea
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a probability geometric construction of generalized exponential families based on probability coordinate charts. A classical exponential family on the unit interval is transported to value space through a chart, producing what we call a G-exponential family. The construction changes the geometry in which exponential structure is represented while leaving the exponential function itself unchanged. This distinguishes it from the algebraic deformations used in the Tsallis and Kaniadakis frameworks. The transported families inherit the structure of the probability coordinate framework. The probability coordinate of each family member follows exactly the original exponential family on the unit interval. Initial Kolmogorov moments are therefore obtained by pulling classical coordinate moments back to value space. For the canonical family, the probability barycenter is the pullback of the mean parameter, while the Fisher information coincides with the Kolmogorov variance. Tail behaviour is inherited from the chart. Every family member is tail equivalent to the chart density, so heavy tails arise from geometry and remain unchanged in order under probability coordinate tilting. This is the opposite of classical exponential tilting. The sufficient statistic is bounded by construction, maximum likelihood reduces to moment matching in probability coordinates, and the maximum likelihood estimator has a bounded influence function. Thus robustness arises from geometric compactification. We also characterise G-exponential families as minimisers of relative entropy to the chart law under coordinate moment constraints and prove that transport preserves the information geometry of the family. A Cauchy chart example and a Monte Carlo study confirm efficient, calibrated, and bounded influence estimation even though every family member has an infinite mean.
tldr: Introduces G-exponential families via probability coordinate charts, altering geometry without changing the exponential function, and shows they minimize relative entropy under moment constraints.
motivation: To generalize exponential families using probability coordinates and achieve robust estimation with heavy tails, distinguishing from algebraic deformations like Tsallis and Kaniadakis.
method: Transports classical exponential families from the unit interval to value space via probability coordinate charts, defining G-exponential families and analyzing their statistical and geometric properties.
result: G-exponential families inherit probability coordinate structure, with Fisher information equal to Kolmogorov variance and tail behavior determined by the chart, yielding bounded-influence MLE even with infinite mean.
conclusion: The geometrical construction offers a novel way to design families with controlled tail behavior and robustness, supported by Cauchy chart example and Monte Carlo studies.

title: Iterative Semantic Decoding For Short Block Codes
authors: Jiafu Hao, Chentao Yue, Mingcheng Nie, Branka Vucetic, Yonghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes an iteratively enhanced semantic receiver for natural-language text transmission over noisy wireless channels using multiple short block codes. At the transmitter, each sentence is permuted by a character-level interleaver, partitioned into segments, and independently encoded by short block codes. At the receiver, we develop an iterative decoder consisting of a channel decoder and a language model, where a de-interleaver between them disperses the burst decoding errors within each segment across the sentence. In each iteration, the language model denoises the channel decoding output, and the denoised characters verified to be consistent with the channel observations are fed back to the channel decoder as semantic information for the next iteration. Simulation results on the Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) corpus over the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel show that the proposed receiver achieves approximately 1.5 dB block error rate (BLER) gain over conventional short-block coding, while maintaining BLEU and ROUGE scores above 99% at SNRs beyond 1.0 dB.
tldr: This paper proposes an iterative semantic decoding scheme for short block codes that combines channel decoding with a language model to improve block error rate for text transmission over noisy channels.
motivation: To improve the reliability of natural-language text transmission over noisy wireless channels using short block codes by exploiting semantic information.
method: The transmitter interleaves characters, partitions sentences into segments, and encodes with short block codes. The receiver uses an iterative decoder that alternates between channel decoding and a language model, feeding back consistent denoised characters to enhance the next iteration.
result: Achieves approximately 1.5 dB BLER gain over conventional short-block coding, with BLEU and ROUGE scores above 99% at SNRs beyond 1.0 dB.
conclusion: Semantic information from language models can significantly enhance the decoding of short block codes in noisy channels.

title: Semi-discrete Quadratic Wasserstein Energy And State-dependent Langevin Exploration
authors: Ran Gu, Gaoyue Guo, Kelvin Shuangjian Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the semi-discrete quadratic Wasserstein energy. The energy is nonsmooth at collisions of sites. We prove local Lipschitz continuity on the full configuration space, together with global semiconcavity, coercivity, and dissipativity; show that every global minimizer is interior and collision free; and establish [MATH] regularity on the collision-free configuration space. The gradient is expressed through the barycenters of the balanced Laguerre cells, while the Hessian is given by an explicit facet formula and satisfies a global one-sided bound. We also solve the one-dimensional problem explicitly in each ordering chamber and give a two-site example on the unit square with non-minimizing Lloyd fixed points. For [MATH], we then formulate an entropy-regularized relaxed control of the Langevin temperature. The controlled dynamics is strongly well posed, nonexplosive, and collision free. Its value function is a classical interior solution of the exploratory Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation; the Laplacian of the value function is locally [MATH], which yields a locally Lipschitz optimal temperature feedback. Independently of this optimal-control result, for every fixed Borel temperature rule bounded away from zero, and every sufficiently small step size, the associated Gaussian Euler chain is geometrically ergodic with a full-support invariant law. The raw iterates do not converge, whereas the best-so-far energy converges almost surely to the global minimum and the running record approaches the set of global minimizers.
tldr: This paper theoretically analyzes a semi-discrete quadratic Wasserstein energy and a state-dependent Langevin exploration algorithm, proving regularity and convergence properties.
motivation: The work aims to understand and provide guarantees for optimization methods based on Langevin dynamics when minimizing non-smooth energies with collisions.
method: The authors prove analytical properties of the energy (Lipschitz continuity, semiconcavity, etc.), characterize the gradient and Hessian via Laguerre cells, and analyze a controlled Langevin process with an entropy-regularized temperature.
result: They establish local Lipschitz continuity, global semiconcavity, coercivity, dissipativity, and regularity of global minimizers; the controlled dynamics is well-posed and collision-free, with geometric ergodicity for fixed step sizes.
conclusion: The paper provides theoretical foundations for a class of stochastic optimization algorithms, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Divergence Of Decreasing Rearranged Fourier Series On Every Infinite Compact Abelian Group
authors: Morten Nielsen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On every infinite compact Hausdorff abelian group there is a complex-valued continuous function whose Fourier sums, taken over coefficients above a decreasing magnitude threshold, are unbounded almost everywhere. In fact, such functions form a dense \(G_\delta\) in the space of continuous functions with its uniform norm. Moreover, a divergent example may be chosen with Fourier support contained in any prescribed infinite subgroup of the dual, while avoiding any prescribed finite set of frequencies. No metrizability or zero-dimensionality is assumed. The proof combines K\"orner's finite circle and Walsh lemmas with a finite construction on products of odd cyclic groups. A trichotomy for the dual group, exact quotient transfer, and cyclic sampling give finite examples on every group under consideration.
tldr: The paper proves that on any infinite compact Hausdorff abelian group, there exist continuous functions whose decreasing-rearranged Fourier series diverge almost everywhere.
motivation: To extend classical results on divergence of rearranged Fourier series from the circle to all infinite compact abelian groups, including non-metrizable settings.
method: Combines K{\"o}rner's finite circle and Walsh lemmas with finite constructions on products of odd cyclic groups, using a trichotomy for the dual group and exact quotient transfer.
result: Establishes that such divergent functions form a dense G_delta set in the space of continuous functions, and can be chosen with Fourier support in any prescribed infinite subgroup of the dual, avoiding any finite set of frequencies.
conclusion: Shows that divergence phenomena for decreasing rearrangements are universal across all infinite compact abelian groups, requiring no metrizability or zero-dimensionality assumptions.

title: Nash-Bargaining HalpernSGD Via Limited-Memory MultiLRSGA: A Two-Phase Optimizer For Multi-Objective Learning
authors: Katherine Rossella Foglia, Francesco Sergio Pisani, Vittorio Colao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose NB-HalpernSGD via LM-MultiLRSGA, a two-phase optimizer for multi-objective optimization. The process starts with a competitive optimization phase by applying a limited-memory variant of MultiLRSGA, named LM-MultiLRSGA, designed to reduce the memory footprint of the original optimizer while preserving its rotational correction mechanism. It addresses multi-objective tasks by considering the competitive game associated with the original multi-objective problem, approximating a Nash equilibrium. This point defines a Nash-equilibrium-induced disagreement point: we formulate the Nash bargaining problem associated with the original losses and rewrite its Nash product as a logarithmic minimization surrogate. This minimization problem is solved using HalpernSGD, anchored at the computed competitive reference point. Therefore, the method uses the Nash equilibrium as a principled reference point for the bargaining stage and then moves toward a Pareto-oriented solution of the original multi-objective problem. We validate the proposed optimizer on a PINN-inspired neural model, where it outperforms established multi-objective optimizers, including PCGrad, MultiAdam, and DualConeGD. Finally, while the convergence properties of HalpernSGD have been extensively studied, we discuss the convergence and stability properties of the proposed LM-MultiLRSGA phase.
tldr: This paper proposes a two-phase optimizer for multi-objective optimization combining Nash bargaining with HalpernSGD, validated on a PINN-inspired model.
motivation: To improve multi-objective optimization by leveraging Nash bargaining and a stable reference point from a competitive phase.
method: Uses a limited-memory variant of MultiLRSGA for the competitive phase, then solves a Nash bargaining problem with HalpernSGD anchored at the Nash equilibrium.
result: Outperforms established multi-objective optimizers like PCGrad, MultiAdam, and DualConeGD on a PINN model, with theoretical convergence discussion for LM-MultiLRSGA.
conclusion: The proposed optimizer shows promise for multi-objective learning tasks, though it is unrelated to the research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: SecDT: A Profile-Based Security Layer For Trdp Communications
authors: Erlantz Alonso, Igor Lopez, Jasone Astorga
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Train Real-time Data Protocol (TRDP) is widely used on rolling stock but it provides limited native support for cryptographic protection. Furthermore, the multicast traffic profile used in TRDP Process Data to exchange critical information between onboard subsystems makes the introduction of cryptographic protection a challenge. This paper presents a lightweight security layer for secure TRDP communication that implements a number of security profiles built around modern cryptographic algorithms. This additional layer relies on an On-board Key Management System (OKMS) for both security profile negotiation, dynamic key distribution and key lifecycle management. The security profiles allow for cryptographic agility and flexibility, ranging from simple authentication to Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms. The security profile negotiation procedure guarantees all TRDP End Devices (ED) on a common Communication ID (ComID) share the same security profile and can therefore process each other's messages. A prototype implementation based on mbedTLS and Arm Platform Security Architecture (PSA) was developed and evaluated. Experimental results demonstrate manageable overhead, suitable for the real-time and time-sensitive communication found on rolling stock.
tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight security layer for TRDP train communication, using cryptographic profiles and an on-board key management system.
motivation: TRDP lacks native cryptographic protection, and the multicast profile used for critical data exchange makes it challenging to secure.
method: The authors design a security layer with predefined security profiles, dynamic key distribution via an On-board Key Management System (OKMS), and use mbedTLS and PSA for implementation.
result: A prototype demonstrates manageable overhead, suitable for real-time train communication.
conclusion: The proposed layer enhances TRDP security with flexibility and cryptographic agility, meeting real-time constraints.

title: Race-aimc: Selective Inference For Heterogeneous Analog In-Memory Accelerators At The Edge
authors: Martin Lueker-Boden Osama Yousuf
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) speeds up neural-network inference by doing the arithmetic directly inside a memory array, instead of shuttling weights back and forth between memory and a processor. This saves energy, but the physical devices that store the weights are imperfect: programming errors, electrical noise, limited-resolution converters, and outright broken cells all distort the computation, and every physical chip is distorted in its own way. A designer with several such chips available faces an uncomfortable choice: run all of them and combine the answers (safe, but wasteful of energy), or trust a single chip blindly (cheap, but with no guarantee on how often it is wrong). This paper introduces RACE-AIMC (Risk-Aware Certified Ensemble for AIMC), a framework that resolves this choice with statistics rather than guesswork. Offline, RACE-AIMC studies a pool of physical accelerators, picks the single best one for a given energy budget, and computes a mathematically exact upper bound on how often that accelerator will be wrong when it chooses to answer. Online, only that one accelerator is switched on; a lightweight check decides whether to accept its answer or defer to a fallback. In our simulations using a noisy weight mapping and multiple independent test runs, every certified bound stayed under a 10% error target (mean bound 7.83% +- 0.89%, with 70.88% +- 0.98% of inputs answered directly). The resulting system matches the accuracy of a clean digital baseline while cutting modeled energy use by 69.02% relative to always running every accelerator in the pool.
tldr: RACE-AIMC is a framework that uses statistical risk-aware selection to pick a single heterogeneous analog in-memory accelerator from a pool, providing certified error bounds to achieve energy-efficient inference on edge devices.
motivation: Analog in-memory computing offers energy efficiency but suffers from device imperfections and variability, forcing designers to choose between using all chips (safe but wasteful) or a single chip (energy-efficient but without error guarantees).
method: Offline, RACE-AIMC studies a pool of accelerators, selects the best one for a given energy budget, and computes a mathematically exact upper bound on its error rate. Online, only that accelerator runs, with a lightweight check to decide whether to accept its answer or defer to a fallback.
result: Simulations with noisy weight mappings showed certified bounds under 10% error (mean 7.83% ± 0.89%), with 70.88% of inputs answered directly, matching a clean digital baseline while reducing modeled energy use by 69.02% relative to always running all accelerators.
conclusion: RACE-AIMC provides a practical statistical solution for reliable use of heterogeneous analog accelerators at the edge, balancing energy savings and accuracy without sacrificing correctness.

title: QSVT-Based Three-Phase Unbalanced Power Flow
authors: Peng Zhang Kamini Shahare
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This letter introduces QSVT-3PF, a quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) based solver for three-phase unbalanced power flow with embedded single-phase grid-forming inverter (GFM) operation. The contributions are threefold: 1) reformulating the Newton correction as a QSVT-compatible inverse problem using a normalized block-encoded phase-domain Jacobian; 2) introducing a regularized singular-value filter to improve robustness under ill-conditioned and stressed operating conditions; and 3) validating the proposed solver on an IEEE 5-bus system and the IEEE 123-node test feeder with single-phase GFM integration. Test results show that QSVT-3PF matches the classical Newton benchmark in residual convergence, voltage profile, and final operating point, demonstrating the feasibility of QSVT-3 for large, unbalanced distribution systems.
tldr: This paper applies quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) to solve three-phase unbalanced power flow, demonstrating feasibility but not contributing to the user's specific research areas.
motivation: Large-scale power flow computations are challenging; quantum algorithms like QSVT may offer computational advantages.
method: The Newton correction is reformulated as a QSVT-compatible inverse problem using block encoding, with a regularized singular-value filter for robustness, and validated on IEEE test systems.
result: The QSVT-based solver matches the classical Newton benchmark in residual convergence, voltage profile, and final operating point.
conclusion: QSVT is feasible for large unbalanced distribution systems, but practical quantum hardware remains a limitation.

title: Privacy, Robustness, And Fairness Trade-offs In Federated Intrusion Detection: Geometric Indistinguishability At The Aggregation Interface
authors: Adrita Rahman Tory, ABM Shawkat Ali, Md Abu Layek, Khondokar Fida Hasan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning enables privacy-conscious collaboration for network intrusion detection without centralizing sensitive traffic data, yet its deployment in operational environments must simultaneously satisfy three competing requirements: formal differential privacy guaranties, tolerance to Byzantine-adversarial participants, and reliable detection coverage across severely imbalanced attack categories. Existing literature treats these properties as independently composable, an assumption that this paper challenges both theoretically and empirically. In this paper, we study how these requirements interact in class-imbalanced federated NIDS and introduce geometric indistinguishability as a conceptual lens for a regime in which privacy-induced dispersion in client updates can make minority-class signals harder for robust aggregation to preserve. Using UNSW-NB15 as a case study, we evaluate DP-SGD combined with coordinate-wise median under label-flip and model-poisoning attacks, with threat coverage assessed across attack categories. Our results provide initial evidence that the joint use of privacy noise and robust aggregation can disproportionately degrade detection of rare attacks relative to majority classes. We also show that part of the observed collapse under strong privacy can arise from training miscalibration, while a residual performance floor may remain for ultra-rare categories even after epsilon-dependent tuning. These findings motivate studying privacy, robustness, and rare-attack coverage jointly rather than as independently composable properties, and suggest that aggregation-aware modeling and sample-aware evaluation are promising directions for trustworthy federated NIDS.
tldr: This paper studies the trade-offs between privacy, robustness, and fairness in federated intrusion detection, showing that DP-SGD with robust aggregation degrades detection of rare attacks.
motivation: The authors aim to address the challenge of satisfying privacy, robustness, and coverage of imbalanced attack classes simultaneously in federated learning for intrusion detection, challenging the assumption that these properties are independent.
method: They apply DP-SGD combined with coordinate-wise median to a federated NIDS, simulating label-flip and model-poisoning attacks, and evaluate on the UNSW-NB15 dataset across attack categories.
result: Initial evidence indicates that the joint use of privacy noise and robust aggregation disproportionately degrades detection of rare attacks; part of the degradation is due to training miscalibration, while a residual performance floor remains for ultra-rare categories.
conclusion: Privacy, robustness, and rare-attack coverage should be studied jointly, and aggregation-aware modeling and sample-aware evaluation are promising directions for trustworthy federated NIDS.

title: Promise Systems Of Equations Over Magmas With Identity And Over Algebras In Congruence Modular Varieties
authors: Nick Jamesson
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the computational complexity of solving promise systems of equations over finite algebras. Given two algebras [MATH] and [MATH] with a homomorphism from [MATH] to [MATH], the promise system of equations problem is to determine if an input system of equations has a solution in [MATH] or not even in [MATH]. We generalize the results of Larrauri, Mottet, and ivn\'y [ACM ToCL'26] to obtain a [MATH]-hard dichotomy result for promise systems of equations over a class of algebras which contains all monoids, and a dichotomy result for promise systems of equations over algebras in a congruence modular variety. We then consider the metaproblem for promise systems of equations over algebras in a congruence modular variety: given finite algebras [MATH] and [MATH] such that [MATH] is in a congruence modular variety, we show there is a quasi-polynomial time algorithm for determining whether or not the associated promise system of equations problem is in [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of promise systems of equations over finite algebras, proving dichotomy results for certain algebraic classes and a quasi-polynomial time metaproblem algorithm.
motivation: To generalize previous dichotomy results for promise CSPs to broader algebraic structures, including monoids and algebras in congruence modular varieties, and to investigate the decidability of the dichotomy classification.
method: The authors employ algebraic and computational complexity techniques, building on prior work by Larrauri et al. to establish dichotomy theorems for promise equation systems over specific classes of algebras, and derive a quasi-polynomial time algorithm for the associated metaproblem.
result: Obtained a hardness dichotomy for promise systems of equations over a class of algebras containing all monoids, another for algebras in congruence modular varieties, and a quasi-polynomial time method to decide if a given instance belongs to P.
conclusion: The work advances the theoretical understanding of promise CSPs and algebraic structures, but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Otter: A Provably MEV-Resilient Automated Market Maker Via Surplus Redistribution
authors: Elaine Shi, Mengqian Zhang, Hao Chung, Yuhao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Miner extractable value (MEV) in automated market makers allows block builders to profit from transaction ordering and injected trades, imposing costs on users and contributing to builder centralization. We introduce Otter (Optimal Truthful Trading with Excess Redistribution), a two-asset batch AMM that achieves provable MEV resilience when the consensus layer provides censorship resilience and block space is uncongested. Otter makes truthful behavior a dominant strategy for both users and builders. Consequently, a builder cannot profit from strategic deviations, including reordering bids or injecting sybil bids, even when the builder is itself a trader with intrinsic value. Moreover, we show that Otter maximizes social welfare, in a strong sense, within a natural class of mechanisms satisfying the desired game-theoretic properties. To achieve these guarantees, we introduce a new paradigm called surplus redistribution, which provably prevents residual surplus from being captured as MEV by redirecting it to the broader community. Specifically, the pool's output tokens need not be distributed entirely among users in the current batch. Instead, residual surplus may be transferred to a smart contract governed by the decentralized community. The accumulated surplus can be used to benefit community members --- for example, by subsidizing transaction fees, rewarding liquidity providers, or returning assets to the pool. Our approach relies on the underlying consensus layer to provide censorship resilience. We motivate its necessity through an impossibility result showing that the desired game-theoretic guarantees become unattainable when the builder is additionally allowed to censor transactions. Thus, our results also provide a mathematically formal demonstration of how consensus-level security guarantees can fundamentally expand what is achievable at the application layer.
tldr: Otter is a batch AMM that provably resists MEV via surplus redistribution and game-theoretic design when the consensus layer provides censorship resilience.
motivation: MEV in AMMs allows block builders to profit at user expense and drives builder centralization; existing designs fail to eliminate strategic manipulation.
method: Introduces the surplus redistribution paradigm and proves truthful dominant strategies for users and builders, plus an impossibility result showing censorship resilience is necessary.
result: Truthful behavior becomes a dominant strategy, social welfare is maximized within a natural mechanism class, and residual surplus is redirected to the community, preventing MEV.
conclusion: Consensus-layer guarantees such as censorship resilience can fundamentally expand the achievable guarantees at the application layer, as shown by the Otter AMM.

title: The Native-Signature Boundary In Post-Quantum Distributed Authorization
authors: Dariia Porechna
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-quantum signature migration poses a distinct systems problem when authorization is distributed among multiple parties. In native threshold signing, the signature algorithm may determine key generation, share state, preprocessing, interaction, combination, refresh, and recovery. Architectures that evaluate threshold policy outside the native signing relation can reduce this coupling, but their authorization evidence is not accepted by an unchanged native verifier unless a trusted complete-key signer translates approval into a native signature. This paper organizes that design boundary through three properties: native-signature compatibility, unilateral-signing resistance, and threshold-layer agility. We classify specialized threshold signatures, generic MPC signing, distributed hash-based constructions, programmable multisignature and dual-gate authorization, and threshold-authorized HSM signing. A migration impact surface identifies which components change with the signature algorithm. Across the surveyed families, no design simultaneously provides native output, unilateral-signing resistance, and threshold-layer agility. This is an architectural tension, not an impossibility claim, and it clarifies why a replaceable API alone does not make distributed authorization cryptographically agile.
tldr: The paper analyzes the architectural tension in distributed authorization systems when migrating to post-quantum signatures, showing that no design can simultaneously achieve native-signature compatibility, unilateral-signing resistance, and threshold-layer agility.
motivation: Post-quantum signature migration is challenging when authorization is distributed, and existing architectures that decouple policy from native signing face compatibility issues with unchanged verifiers.
method: The paper defines three properties (native-signature compatibility, unilateral-signing resistance, threshold-layer agility) and classifies various families of threshold signatures and distributed authorization schemes.
result: Across all surveyed families, no design simultaneously provides all three properties, indicating an inherent architectural tension rather than an impossibility.
conclusion: The identified tension explains why a replaceable API alone is insufficient for cryptographic agility in distributed authorization, highlighting a fundamental systems design challenge.

title: Random Garbage Separates Xor From Forward-Only Queries
authors: Khaled Elbassioni, Rishikesh Gajjala, Saurabh Ray
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give exponential quantum query separations between the standard XOR interface and two forward-only interfaces that supply neither an adjoint nor an inverse oracle. Let [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], where [MATH] is promised to be either a permutation or a Simon two-to-one function, and [MATH] is a fixed table of [MATH]-bit tags, unrestricted by the promise and reused on every query. The resulting problem is solvable with at most [MATH] standard XOR queries, but has forward-erasing query complexity [MATH]. This answers affirmatively open question 11 in [Scott Aaronson. Open problems related to quantum query complexity. ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing, 2(4):14:1-14:9, 2021] . We also embed these instances into permutations. The detailed construction retains the copy of [MATH] in each prescribed output, but for these promises that copy can be replaced by one bit that distinguishes the two inputs in every Simon pair. This gives a permutation domain of size [MATH] and a permutation problem with the same standard-query upper bound and forward-only in-place query complexity [MATH]. Both lower bounds remain valid with a clean coherent bypass. The common lower bound uses an analysis-only recording replacement. In the replacement computation, tracing out the fixed random tag table after [MATH] calls gives a sum of positive-semidefinite operator contributions, each depending on [MATH] at no more than [MATH] addresses. On such a set, the restrictions induced by random permutations and random Simon functions differ only if the set contains a hidden Simon pair, an event of probability [MATH].
tldr: This paper proves exponential separations between standard XOR quantum queries and forward-only query interfaces for a promise problem based on Simon's problem, answering an open question in quantum query complexity.
motivation: To understand the power of different quantum query interfaces, specifically the limitations when no adjoint or inverse oracle is available.
method: The authors construct a promise problem where the function is either a permutation or a Simon function, augmented with a fixed random tag table, and analyze the query complexity for standard XOR versus forward-only interfaces.
result: They show that the problem can be solved with only a few standard XOR queries but requires exponentially many forward-only queries, providing a clear separation.
conclusion: The results answer open question 11 in Aaronson's list and establish robust lower bounds that hold even with coherent bypass techniques.

title: Security And Privacy In The Musical Metaverse: Threat Analysis And Design Implications
authors: Micha{\l} K{\l}osinski Luca Turchet
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Musical Metaverse (MM) introduces immersive, real-time environments for collaborative musical interaction, characterized by ultra-low-latency constraints, continuous multimodal data streams, and heterogeneous devices. These properties create a distinctive security and privacy landscape that differs significantly from conventional XR or multimedia systems. This paper presents a multi-layer threat analysis of MM ecosystems, identifying key assets including live musical content, expressive interaction data, identity and session metadata, and intellectual property. Threats are analyzed across network, application, data/AI, device, intellectual property rights, and social layers, with particular attention to risks arising from expressive and neurophysiological data, which enable inference, re-identification, and potential privacy violations. We describe a stakeholder-driven survey involving 14 participants from 13 organizations, revealing that neurophysiological data leakage and real-time stream disruption are perceived as the most critical risks, followed by intellectual property infringement and avatar impersonation. We further evaluate the suitability of existing security protocols under strict latency constraints, showing that conventional approaches such as TLS over TCP are often incompatible with real-time musical interaction, while lightweight, stream-oriented mechanisms (e.g., SRTP, DTLS) provide a more suitable balance between security and performance. Based on these findings, we derive a set of design guidelines for MM systems, emphasizing latency-aware security, differentiation of interaction paths, data minimization, and edge-centric processing. The results support a security-by-design approach that enables trust and compliance without compromising real-time performance.
tldr: This paper presents a multi-layer threat analysis of the Musical Metaverse, identifying privacy and security risks and deriving design guidelines.
motivation: The Musical Metaverse has unique security and privacy challenges due to real-time interaction, continuous multimodal data streams, and strict latency constraints.
method: The authors conducted a multi-layer threat analysis across network, application, data/AI, device, IPR, and social layers, surveyed 14 stakeholders from 13 organizations, and evaluated existing security protocols under latency constraints.
result: Key perceived risks include neurophysiological data leakage and real-time stream disruption; lightweight stream-oriented protocols like SRTP and DTLS were found more suitable than TLS over TCP.
conclusion: The paper proposes design guidelines emphasizing latency-aware security, data minimization, and edge-centric processing to support security-by-design in Musical Metaverse systems.

title: AlcaTRAz - Anchored Tree-Rule Defense Against Jailbreaks
authors: Jakub Re\v{s}, Petr Ka\v{s}ka, Martin Pere\v{s}\'ini, Martin Ukrop, Kamil Malinka
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that bypass safety alignment through carefully crafted prompts. Many existing defenses require access to model weights or internals, making them difficult to apply to black-box deployments. We propose AlcaTRAz (Anchored Tree-Rule defense Against jailbreaks), a prompt-level defense based on rule trees that operates exclusively on the input text and requires no modification or retraining of the target model. The method automatically learns a transferable transformation rule that inserts controlled character-level perturbations at selected positions, thereby disrupting structural regularities exploited by jailbreak attacks while largely preserving the model's utility on benign queries. We evaluate the proposed method across 33 open-weight models, 22 jailbreak attack types, and a benchmark of short, single-turn benign questions, comparing against three representative prompt-level baselines (Llama Guard, RA-LLM, Goal Prioritization). Among the compared defenses, AlcaTRAz achieves the best composite security and functionality score in 73.4 % of model-attack combinations and shifts the aggregate score from a modal value of 10 (maximal-severity response to the malicious request) in the undefended setting to a modal value of 2 (near-refusal) after defense, while keeping the mean benign score within 0.27 points of the undefended baseline (8.35 vs. 8.62 on a 0-10 scale). AlcaTRAz substantially reduces but does not eliminate jailbreak success: a high-severity tail remains, and we do not consider adaptive attackers, so we position it as one layer within a defense-in-depth strategy rather than a standalone guarantee.
tldr: A prompt-level defense against jailbreaks using character-level perturbations learned from a rule tree, preserving utility while reducing attack success.
motivation: Existing jailbreak defenses require access to model internals, limiting black-box applications; AlcaTRAz aims to defend purely from the input text.
method: AlcaTRAz learns a transferable transformation rule via rule trees that inserts controlled character-level perturbations at selected positions to disrupt jailbreak patterns while maintaining benign utility.
result: Evaluated on 33 models and 22 attack types, AlcaTRAz achieves the best composite score in 73.4% of model-attack combos and shifts modal severity from 10 to 2, with minor benign score drop.
conclusion: The defense substantially reduces but does not eliminate jailbreak risk; it should be used as one layer in a defense-in-depth strategy.

title: A Quantization Problem Posed By Adaptive Streaming
authors: Yuriy A. Reznik

Each client plays the highest rendition that its network bandwidth can sustain. We show that choosing the ladder is a problem of of the bandwidth distribution. However, this quantization problem is of an unusual kind: the client's logic pins each quantization cell's reproduction value to the cell's , and the distortion measure is a one-sided quality loss rather than a squared error. The constraint reshapes the classical theory. The of a ladder is the distance between its average delivered quality and the that infinitely many renditions would attain. For optimal [MATH]-rendition ladders the gap [MATH] decays as [MATH], not the textbook [MATH]. Moreover, with large [MATH], [MATH], with the limit attained when the ladder's rates follow the density [MATH], which replaces Panter--Dite's [MATH]; here [MATH] is the bandwidth density and [MATH] the quality--rate curve of the content. The law yields closed-form design rules: quantile rung placement, the rendition count [MATH] needed to reach tolerance [MATH], and the economic ladder size [MATH] when a rendition costs [MATH] to operate and the quality gap is priced at [MATH]. The same analysis extends to the design of ladders employing different video resolutions, codecs, perceptual quality metrics, and the two-dimensional adaptation logic of modern web players.
tldr: This paper addresses a quantization problem in adaptive bitrate streaming, deriving optimal encoding ladder design based on bandwidth distribution.
motivation: To optimize the selection of encoding bitrates (ladders) for adaptive streaming to maximize delivered quality given bandwidth constraints.
method: Formulates ladder selection as a quantization problem with a one-sided distortion measure and derives asymptotic laws for optimal ladders.
result: Finds that the gap between average delivered quality and ideal decays as a different power law, and provides closed-form design rules for ladder placement.
conclusion: The analysis can extend to other dimensions like resolution, codec, and multidimensional adaptation.

title: Rent-a-RAG: Embedding-Space Watermarks For Auditing Third-Party Rag
authors: Alexandr Goultiaev Tolstokorov, Kyriakos Mouratidis, Javad Dogani, Nikolaos Laoutaris
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Third-party retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) marketplaces create a new auditing problem: data providers may license corpora to a RAG operator, yet later have no visibility into whether their documents are being reused without compensation. Auditing this misuse is difficult because the operator is non-cooperative, answers are paraphrased by the generator, and one response may combine evidence from many providers. We propose DirBucket, a provider-side semantic watermarking and black-box auditing framework for document-level reuse in multi-provider RAG. DirBucket watermarks documents by meaning-preserving paraphrases whose embeddings are biased toward provider-bucket secret directions, enabling detection from black-box answers while preserving retrieval utility. On a challenging benchmark that reflects mixed-provider reuse under black-box access, DirBucket is the only method that consistently achieves strong target detection with no non-target activation, detecting non-compliance in every audit within 23 audited answers on our primary benchmark. The watermark survives adversarial post-answer laundering, and none of the evaluated evasion strategies simultaneously defeats detection while preserving user-perceived answer quality. Detection transfers unchanged to a second benchmark built from real clinical, cyber-threat-intelligence, and legal provider corpora. These results suggest that embedding-space watermarking can make document reuse in third-party RAG statistically auditable.
tldr: Proposes DirBucket, an embedding-space watermarking framework for auditing document reuse in third-party RAG systems.
motivation: To enable data providers to detect unauthorized reuse of their licensed corpora in non-cooperative RAG marketplaces where answers are paraphrased and combine evidence from multiple providers.
method: Watermarks documents by meaning-preserving paraphrases biased toward provider-bucket secret directions in embedding space, enabling black-box detection from generated answers.
result: DirBucket achieves strong target detection with no non-target activation, detecting non-compliance within 23 audited answers, and remains robust to adversarial laundering and transferable to real corpora.
conclusion: Embedding-space watermarking can make document reuse in third-party RAG statistically auditable.

title: Inferring Hidden User Models From The Behavior Of Personalized Llm Agents
authors: Haoyang Li, Yaxin Xiao, Qingqing Ye, Huadi Zheng, Haibo Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent personalized LLM agents increasingly transform information retained in memory into compressed or structured representations, which we call user models, to guide later decisions. When source wording is removed from the state reachable through the ordinary interface, these models are commonly treated as more privacy-preserving because direct memory-extraction attacks lose the text they target. Yet we argue that user models expose a new attack surface because an attacker can still recover the private information from the personalized choices they shape, even when source records and backend state remain inaccessible. We therefore introduce UMPeek, a black-box attack based on hypothesis-guided adaptive probing to infer such hidden user model. It forms hypotheses from choices left open by a request, switches among ordinary follow-up tasks, and retains only claims supported and not contradicted by visible behavior. We conduct an extensive benchmark evaluation across diverse personalization tasks and user-model backends against existing attacks. We further validate UMPeek in real-world systems using information confirmed to be retained, and we evaluate defenses against its adaptive probing. Overall, UMPeek outperforms existing attacks in both benchmark and real-world comparisons and continues to recover user information under response-level defenses, showing that keeping records and backend state inaccessible does not guarantee semantic privacy when retained information shapes visible behavior.
tldr: The paper introduces UMPeek, a black-box attack that infers hidden user models in personalized LLM agents by adaptive probing, demonstrating that semantic privacy is compromised even when source records are inaccessible.
motivation: Personalized LLM agents often transform retained information into user models, which are assumed to be more privacy-preserving; however, the authors argue that observable behavior can expose private information through these models.
method: UMPeek employs hypothesis-guided adaptive probing, forming hypotheses from response choices and alternating among follow-up tasks to validate retained user model claims based on visible behavior.
result: UMPeek outperforms existing attacks in both benchmark and real-world evaluations, and it continues to recover user information even when response-level defenses are in place.
conclusion: Keeping records and backend state inaccessible does not guarantee semantic privacy, as retained information that shapes visible behavior can be inferred through adaptive probing.

title: Flip, Don't Shuffle: Watermarking LLMs At The Speed Of Inference
authors: Ignacio Sanchez Simone Ceppi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Stateless Bernoulli Watermarking (SBW), a new statistical watermark for Large Language Models that determines green list membership through independent per-token Bernoulli trials. Unlike KGW's vocabulary permutation or SynthID's multi-layer tournament, SBW requires only a single comparison per token against a counter-based random number generator, reducing membership complexity to [MATH] and enabling single-kernel execution with zero intermediate allocations. We prove that this formulation preserves the same detection guarantees as fixed-size green lists: the z-score test remains [MATH] under the null. The stateless architecture enables capabilities unavailable to existing methods: full-vocabulary self-salt watermarking (over 6000[MATH] faster than KGW's self-salt and 2[MATH] faster than SynthID despite biasing the entire vocabulary with candidate-dependent seeding) and architectural compatibility with distributed inference. In end-to-end generation benchmarks, SBW adds less than 1\% overhead at all batch sizes. We additionally identify hash function design as a previously unexplored axis for watermark quality, showing that a GPU-native Jenkins hash improves null calibration by 1.8[MATH] while producing more diverse text. Experiments across two seeding schemes and eight [MATH] configurations confirm statistical equivalence with ROC-AUC differences below 0.01.
tldr: Introduces Stateless Bernoulli Watermarking (SBW) for LLMs, a faster and more efficient method for embedding and detecting watermarks during inference.
motivation: Existing watermarking methods (KGW, SynthID) are computationally expensive and hinder inference speed; there is a need for a low-overhead, scalable watermarking technique.
method: SBW determines green list membership via independent per-token Bernoulli trials using a counter-based RNG, requiring a single comparison per token and enabling single-kernel execution with no intermediate allocations.
result: SBW adds less than 1% overhead at all batch sizes, is faster than existing methods (especially in self-salt configurations), and maintains statistical equivalence with ROC-AUC differences below 0.01.
conclusion: SBW offers a practical and efficient watermarking solution for LLMs, with potential compatibility for distributed inference and improved hash design.

title: The Head Complexity Of Boolean Functions In Single-Layer Attention
authors: Rajmohan Rajaraman, Ravi Sundaram, Amanuel Tesfaye
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What can a single layer of self-attention compute? We study head complexity: the minimum number of attention heads required to compute a function in a one-layer attention-only model. We establish an exact hierarchy under this measure: [MATH] heads compute [MATH]-bit parity but cannot compute [MATH]-bit parity. The lower bound is unconditional in the two resources a transformer might otherwise exploit; it holds at unbounded embedding dimension and unbounded numerical precision. The proof rests on an alternating-sum obstruction: after clearing the softmax denominators, every monomial in the resulting decision polynomial omits at least one of the [MATH] input bits, forcing its correlation with parity to vanish. The same obstruction yields lower bounds for related tasks, including the well-studied multi-hop induction-head task. We also establish compactness bounds for embedding dimension and numerical precision. Specifically, a compactness theorem shows that any function computable at all can be computed with embedding dimension and precision bounded by the discrete data of the task, namely, head count, alphabet size, and length. Thus, potentially unbounded dimension or precision provably cannot substitute for heads. Finally, we derive nearly matching universal bounds for general binary functions: [MATH] heads suffice to compute every [MATH]-bit binary function, with one head per monomial in its multilinear expansion, while a counting argument shows almost all such functions require [MATH] heads. This lower bound matches the upper bound to within a [MATH] factor, even when dimension and precision are unbounded. Together, these results characterize head requirements for Boolean computation in this model.
tldr: This paper characterizes the minimum number of attention heads needed in a single-layer attention-only transformer to compute Boolean functions, establishing a hierarchy and universal bounds.
motivation: Understanding the computational limits of transformer architectures, specifically what can be computed with a fixed number of attention heads.
method: They use an alternating-sum obstruction and counting arguments to prove lower and upper bounds on head complexity.
result: They establish exact bounds for parity, show that unbounded embedding dimension or precision cannot substitute for heads, and provide nearly matching universal bounds for arbitrary Boolean functions.
conclusion: The results provide a precise characterization of the computational power of single-layer attention in terms of head count.

title: Variational Probabilistic Quantization For Secret Key Generation
authors: Xinyang Li, Vlad C. Andrei, Peter J. Gu, Yiqi Chen, Ullrich J. M\"onich, Holger Boche
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secret key generation from correlated observations at Alice and Bob, in the presence of an eavesdropper Eve, underpins physical-layer security. Classical pipelines quantize by hand, amplify privacy afterwards, and optimize no objective tied to a key rate. We propose Variational Probabilistic Quantization (VPQ): neural encoders that map the correlated sources directly into a discrete key alphabet, trained by a variational adversarial objective whose entropy, mismatch, and leakage terms match the three terms of the one-way secret key rate. A linear code-offset secure sketch then reconciles the encoder outputs into an identical key without a separate privacy amplification step. We prove that the VPQ losses lower-bound the one-way secret key capacity of the induced source, and derive in closed form the optimal worst-case key rate over the source class of a given alphabet size and mismatch probability, attained by finite-field linear sketches. On Gaussian fading channels, VPQ leaks less to a correlated eavesdropper than one classical and two recent learning-based baselines, and Reed--Solomon reconciliation operates within the predicted finite-blocklength gap.
tldr: VPQ uses neural encoders with a variational adversarial objective to directly map correlated sources to key alphabets, optimizing the one-way secret key rate and using secure sketches for reconciliation.
motivation: Classical quantization and privacy amplification in secret key generation are hand-crafted and not optimized for key rate; VPQ aims for end-to-end optimization.
method: Neural encoders learn a probabilistic mapping from sources to a discrete alphabet, trained with an objective matching entropy, mismatch, and leakage terms of the secret key rate; secure sketches reconcile encoder outputs.
result: On Gaussian fading channels, VPQ outperforms classical and learning-based baselines in leakage, and Reed-Solomon reconciliation approaches the finite-blocklength bound.
conclusion: VPQ provides a novel, principled framework for secret key generation with provable lower bounds and superior performance.

title: Dipolar Order Across Bravais Lattice Space: Classification, Spin Waves, And A Four-attractor Phase Diagram
authors: Josep Batle
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every crystal is a Bravais lattice decorated by a basis, so the dipolar ordering of the fourteen Bravais lattices is the natural starting point for any systematic theory of dipolar magnetism in three dimensions. We determine it here in a single common framework: the interaction tensor is Ewald-summed, the classical ground state is obtained by minimising the lowest Luttinger--Tisza band over the entire Brillouin zone, and the linear spin-wave spectrum with its zero-point corrections is computed for every lattice whose order is collinear. Three results emerge that are not properties of individual lattices but of the landscape. First, two structural principles --- the exact tracelessness of the dipolar tensor in three dimensions, and its identical vanishing at [MATH] for every cubic-symmetric lattice --- explain the ordering type, the absence of first-order cubic anisotropy, and the systematics of the zero-point moment reduction. Second, exactly one lattice defeats the Luttinger--Tisza construction: for face-centred orthorhombic the optimal eigenvector is not circular, the single-[MATH] state is a spin-density wave of non-constant length, and the tabulated energy is a strict lower bound; direct supercell minimisation gives the true ground state. Third, optimising each family over its free metric parameters collapses the whole of Bravais space onto only attractors, with body-centred tetragonal the global optimum and a single interior optimum at rhombohedral [MATH] lying below face-centred cubic. Three independent published benchmarks are reproduced.
tldr: This paper classifies dipolar ordering across all fourteen Bravais lattices, identifying structural principles and a phase diagram with four attractors.
motivation: To provide a systematic understanding of dipolar magnetism in crystals by analyzing the ground states and excitations of all Bravais lattices.
method: Ewald summation for the dipolar interaction, Luttinger-Tisza minimization, linear spin-wave analysis, and direct supercell minimization for cases where the Luttinger-Tisza construction fails.
result: Identifies two structural principles governing ordering, demonstrates a failure for face-centred orthorhombic, and shows that Bravais lattices collapse onto four attractors with body-centred tetragonal as the global optimum.
conclusion: Offers a comprehensive classification and phase diagram for dipolar magnets, but is unrelated to the specified research directions.

title: Constituent-Tagged Transfer Linking Cluster Dynamics To Static Scaling

Tracking the host size of a conserved constituent defines [MATH] by [MATH], with [MATH].
