tldr: The paper proves well-posedness of nonlinear filtering equations in weighted Sobolev spaces with unbounded system coefficients.
motivation: Filtering theory is central to control, but existing well-posedness results often assume bounded coefficients or restrict to simpler spaces.
method: Introduces exponential-type weights and buffered weighted Sobolev spaces, then uses variational techniques for the robust DMZ equation and gauge transformations to handle stochastic DMZ and Kushner-Stratonovich equations.
result: Establishes existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for all three filtering equations under mild, verifiable assumptions on unbounded coefficients.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified treatment that broadens applicability to general nonlinear filtering systems with unbounded coefficients.

title: Combinatorial Search For Strong Shift Equivalence
authors: Emmanuel Jeandel
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The most important open problem of symbolic dynamics consists in finding a procedure to decide whether two subshifts of finite type are conjugate or, equivalently, whether two nonnegative integer matrices are strong shift equivalent. While the problem remains hard in general, the literature also contains specific examples of matrices that are not known to be strong shift equivalent: the Baker matrices, and Ashley's eight-by-eight. These specific examples have been open for 30 years. Using computer experiments, we show that the Baker matrices are indeed strong shift equivalent for small values of k, and that Ashley's eight-by-eight matrix is indeed strong shift equivalent to the one-by-one matrix 2.
tldr: This paper uses computer experiments to attack long-standing open problems in symbolic dynamics by testing strong shift equivalence of specific matrices.
motivation: The most important open problem in symbolic dynamics is deciding conjugacy of subshifts of finite type, equivalent to strong shift equivalence of nonnegative integer matrices. The Baker matrices and Ashley's eight-by-eight matrix have been open for 30 years.
method: The author performs computer searches to check if the matrices are strong shift equivalent for small values of k, likely by searching for explicit equivalence sequences of factorizations.
result: Computer experiments show that the Baker matrices are strong shift equivalent for small k, and Ashley's eight-by-eight matrix is strong shift equivalent to the one-by-one matrix 2.
conclusion: The findings provide strong computational evidence that these matrices may be equivalent, potentially guiding future proofs or algorithmic approaches.

title: Dynamical (non-)recurrence Of Escaping Exponential Maps
authors: Weiwei Cui, Jiaxing Huang, Jun Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that exponential maps could have complicated measurable behaviours by giving two examples in the exponential family both with singular value escaping to infinity ``slowly", one of which is recurrent (in the sense that every positive measure set will return to itself infinitely many times), while the other is non-recurrent. This also complements earlier results of Lyubich, Rees, Urba\'nski-Zdunik, and Hemke. We also give an example of exponential maps with singular value escaping to infinity arbitrarily slow, which is a parametric analog of a result of Rempe.
tldr: The paper shows that exponential maps can have complicated measurable behaviors, providing recurrent and non-recurrent examples with slowly escaping singular values.
motivation: To understand measurable dynamics of exponential maps when the singular value escapes to infinity slowly, complementing earlier work by Lyubich, Rees, Urbański-Zdunik, and Hemke.
method: Constructs specific exponential maps with singular values escaping at different rates and analyzes their recurrence properties using measurable dynamics techniques.
result: Provides examples of recurrent and non-recurrent exponential maps with slow escape, and an example with arbitrarily slow escape analogous to a result by Rempe.
conclusion: The findings demonstrate that exponential maps can exhibit complex measurable dynamics depending on the escape rate of the singular value.

title: On The $\Omega(n)$ Sdp Relaxation Gap For Submodular Box-Constrained Quadratic Programming
authors: Guanyi Wang Junyu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous submodular optimization is an important class of nonconvex problems with global guarantees, for which the submodular box-constrained quadratic programming (BCQP) forms a fundamental subclass. It arises naturally as quadratic subproblems of general twice-differentiable submodular problems and also has direct business and management applications such as pricing. This paper studies the worst-case relaxation gap of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations with a finite family of valid linear cuts for submodular BCQP. We show that in dimension [MATH], for any SDP relaxation formulated with a finite family of linear cuts, there always exists a submodular BCQP instance with a strictly positive relaxation gap. By restricting to the normalized BCQP instances that remove the problem's scaling factor, we further quantify this limitation with explicit lower bounds. In general dimension [MATH], when the SDP relaxation is formulated with only Boolean-quadric-polytope (BQP) valid cuts, including the commonly used McCormick and triangle inequalities, we establish an [MATH] relaxation gap lower bound. For an arbitrary family of [MATH] valid linear cuts, we establish an [MATH] lower bound. These results capture the fundamental limitations of SDP relaxations, especially SDP with BQP valid cuts, and provide guidance on what additional constraints may be needed for more effective convex approximations of submodular BCQP.
tldr: This paper analyzes the worst-case relaxation gap of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations for submodular box-constrained quadratic programming, showing fundamental limitations when using finite families of linear cuts.
motivation: To understand the limits of convex relaxations like SDP for submodular optimization problems, which arise in various applications and as subproblems in global optimization.
method: The authors construct submodular BCQP instances to show that any SDP relaxation with a finite set of linear cuts leaves a strictly positive gap. They also provide explicit lower bounds for cuts from the Boolean quadric polytope (including McCormick and triangle inequalities) and for arbitrary finite cut families.
result: In general dimension n, the gap lower bound is Ω(n) when using BQP valid cuts, and Ω(n) for any finite family of cuts, with tighter bounds for normalized instances.
conclusion: SDP relaxations with only a finite number of linear cuts cannot achieve exactness for all submodular BCQP instances, indicating that richer constraint sets are required for more effective convex approximations.

title: Residual Neural Networks Overcome The Curse Of Dimensionality For Semilinear Heat Equations
authors: Diyora Salimova Ilkhom Mukhammadiev
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rigorous results show that feedforward neural networks can overcome the curse of dimensionality in the numerical approximation of high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs), but comparatively little is known about residual neural networks (ResNets) in the nonlinear PDE setting. We prove that ResNets overcome the curse of dimensionality in the numerical approximation of solutions of semilinear heat equations with globally Lipschitz continuous, gradient-independent nonlinearities: under polynomial growth and network approximability hypotheses on the PDE data, there exist [MATH] and ResNets [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], with at most [MATH] parameters whose realizations approximate the solution in dimension [MATH] with an [MATH]-error of at most [MATH]. The proof represents one deterministic realization of a multilevel Picard estimator by a ResNet whose shortcut connections transmit the spatial variable and a scalar accumulator, while the residual branches successively add the summands of the estimator. For ridge-sum initial conditions, admissible sigmoidal activations, and globally Lipschitz truncations of the nonlinearity, we obtain, for every [MATH], the explicit bound [MATH] on the number of parameters.
tldr: This paper proves that residual neural networks can approximate high-dimensional semilinear heat equations without suffering the curse of dimensionality, given the PDE data satisfy certain smoothness and approximability conditions.
motivation: While feedforward networks are known to overcome the curse of dimensionality for certain PDEs, it was unclear whether residual networks (ResNets) possess the same capability, especially for nonlinear problems.
method: The authors construct explicit ResNet architectures that implement a multilevel Picard estimator, with shortcut connections passing the spatial variable and a scalar accumulator, and analyze the parameter count and approximation error.
result: They show that for semilinear heat equations with globally Lipschitz nonlinearities, there exist ResNets with at most a polynomial number of parameters that achieve epsilon accuracy in high dimension, with explicit bounds under additional assumptions.
conclusion: ResNets can indeed break the curse of dimensionality for this class of PDEs, extending prior results from feedforward networks to residual architectures.

title: Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference For Cognitive Diagnosis
authors: Yagna Manasa Boyapati, Chong Yu, Tianyu Jiang, Justin Zhan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Significant challenges remain in AI-driven educational systems in balancing privacy preservation with accurate cognitive diagnosis. To overcome this, we propose a federated inference framework in which several commercial LLM APIs collaborate without requiring access to raw student data or proprietary model internals. Using multiple federated entities, such as LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, and Claude-3-Haiku, our framework builds upon a heterogeneous multi-LLM architecture. The predictions generated by these entities are combined with epsilon-local differential privacy by adding Laplace noise locally to each entity's prediction output before aggregation, while residual-based aggregation mitigates model heterogeneity. Our approach is predicated on an honest-but-curious trust paradigm in which API providers are presumed not to abuse submitted queries, and our differential privacy mechanism shields the published diagnostic results from external inference. We conduct rigorous privacy-utility analysis showing strong privacy guarantees with minimal accuracy loss, and extensive real-world evaluations across three educational benchmarks confirm the framework's practical usability and cross-domain generalizability.
tldr: A federated inference framework uses multiple commercial LLMs with local differential privacy to perform cognitive diagnosis while protecting student data.
motivation: Education systems need both privacy preservation and accurate cognitive diagnosis, but current methods struggle to balance these.
method: Multiple LLM APIs (LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3-Haiku) generate predictions locally; Laplace noise is added to each output for epsilon-differential privacy, and residual-based aggregation addresses model heterogeneity.
result: The method achieves strong privacy guarantees with minimal accuracy loss and shows practical usability and cross-domain generalizability on three educational benchmarks.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates a viable privacy-preserving approach for multi-model federated inference in educational settings, but it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: PrivateHub: Contrastive Diffusion Model For Private Sensor-Intensive Environment Data Generation
authors: Jiechao Gao, Yuandong Pan, Jie Wang, Michael Lepech, Bradford Campbell
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sensor-intensive environments enable many intelligent services by inferring user applications from heterogeneous data streams. However, not all applications should be exposed: users want some activities to stay private. This creates a tension between inferring applications for useful services and preventing unwanted inference. Existing approaches such as differential privacy and rule-based filtering protect individual streams but cannot address the privacy risk from cross-sensor inference. We introduce Privatehub, which uses contrastive learning within a diffusion model to generate synthetic multi-sensor streams that keep non-private applications detectable while concealing private ones. Privatehub has two stages: App-Conditioned Pre-training (ACP), which conditions the model on multi-sensor data with application embeddings, and App-Aware Fine-tuning (AAF), which separates private from non-private data via contrastive learning. We also define a threat model for the multi-sensor sharing setting. Experiments on three real-world multi-sensor datasets show Privatehub lowers private-application accuracy by 40 to 50\% without hurting non-private performance, and stays robust when the attacker retrains on the synthetic data.
tldr: This paper presents PrivateHub, a contrastive diffusion model that generates synthetic multi-sensor data streams to conceal private applications while preserving non-private ones.
motivation: Sensor-intensive environments rely on cross-sensor inference, but users may want some activities to remain private. Existing methods like differential privacy fail against cross-sensor inference attacks.
method: PrivateHub uses a two-stage approach: App-Conditioned Pre-training (ACP) conditions the diffusion model on sensor data with application embeddings, and App-Aware Fine-tuning (AAF) separates private from non-private data via contrastive learning.
result: Experiments on three real-world datasets show PrivateHub reduces private-application detection accuracy by 40–50% while maintaining non-private performance, and remains robust even if the attacker retrains on the synthetic data.
conclusion: The method effectively generates synthetic multi-sensor streams that hide private activities without compromising the utility of non-private applications.

title: When Optimization Becomes Manipulation: Defending Generative Search Against Malicious Generative Engine Optimization
authors: Haozhang Li, Yangguang Shao, Xinjie Lin, Zhong Guan, Mi Zhou, Junzheng Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper focuses on defending generative search engines against malicious Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), which rewrites web documents to match engines' citation preferences and thereby manipulates generated answers. Recent GEO methods have advanced from hand-crafted rewriting to automated and agentic optimization, substantially increasing the visibility of target documents in generated answers. However, defending against such manipulation poses two major challenges: attack documents remain factually consistent with their originals, rendering fact verification and perplexity filtering ineffective, and the features they amplify equally characterize high-quality benign content. To address these limitations, we propose GEO Defender, a two-stage defense aligned with the attack chain that requires no fine-tuning of the target LLM. GEO Defender consists of Shield Reranker and Training-Free Shield Generation (TFSG). Specifically, Shield Reranker learns a preference-based defensive residual over a frozen base reranker, demoting GEO-rewritten documents while preserving relevance judgments, and TFSG distills defense outcomes into a natural-language experience library that guides the target LLM's source use at inference. Experiments on two state-of-the-art closed-source LLMs and three open-source LLMs across seven GEO attacks demonstrate that GEO Defender reduces the average attack success rate from 50.32% to 6.20%, retains 94.12% of benign-evidence use, preserves answer quality, and generalizes to unseen attacks from construction instances.
tldr: This paper introduces GEO Defender, a two-stage defense against malicious Generative Engine Optimization attacks on generative search engines.
motivation: GEO attacks manipulate search engine outputs by rewriting documents to match citation preferences, and existing defenses fail against factually consistent but manipulated content.
method: GEO Defender combines a Shield Reranker that learns preference-based defensive residuals to demote GEO-rewritten documents, and Training-Free Shield Generation (TFSG) that distills defense outcomes into a natural-language experience library to guide LLM source use.
result: GEO Defender reduces average attack success rate from 50.32% to 6.20%, retains 94.12% of benign-evidence use, preserves answer quality, and generalizes to unseen attacks.
conclusion: The proposed defense effectively mitigates GEO attacks without fine-tuning the target LLM, demonstrating robustness across multiple LLMs and attack types.

title: Boundary-Mutation Testing For Pattern-Based Secret Detection: A Rule-Level Method And Cross-Scanner Evaluation
authors: Shweta Mishra
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pattern-based secret scanners are commonly validated with example-based fixtures that fix one variable: the text surrounding a credential. We introduce boundary-mutation testing to vary that context, generating credentials from each rule's own regular expression, embedding them in realistic source contexts, and classifying outcomes at the rule level rather than the tool level, yielding three detection metrics. Applied to three scanners - a 43-rule open-source scanner, Gitleaks 8.21.2, and TruffleHog 3.82.13 - detection in the primary subject holds at >=0.9976 across ten contexts but collapses to 0.5233 when a credential ends in a hyphen. Five rules are affected: two, with fixed-count quantifiers, fail totally and deterministically; three, with variable-count quantifiers, backtrack and match a truncated credential; an entropy fallback rescues some failures but downgrades their severity. We validate a repair restoring full robustness with no new false positives, and report a caution: a plausible first attempt silently regressed two rules, caught only by re-running the same battery. Gitleaks has an unrelated, source-confirmed defect - a hard-coded terminator allowlist causing total misses for most credential types - while TruffleHog shows no boundary fragility but narrowest coverage. We report marginal, not conditional, failure probabilities: one common token format is structurally immune, another fails once in 64; on 292,527 lines of real code, the false-positive ordering inverts relative to the synthetic corpus. Because per-type detection is deterministic, the comparison unit is ten credential types, not hundreds of samples; no recall difference reaches significance, so we report the null result, not a ranking.
tldr: The paper introduces boundary-mutation testing to evaluate pattern-based secret scanners at a rule level, revealing fragility in certain contexts.
motivation: Traditional example-based fixtures for secret scanners vary only one variable; the paper aims to systematically test scanner robustness across varying contexts and rule-level detection.
method: The method generates credentials from each rule's regular expression, embeds them in realistic source contexts, and classifies detection outcomes at the rule level, producing three detection metrics.
result: Applied to three scanners, detection held in most contexts but dropped to 0.5233 when credentials end in a hyphen, affecting five rules; a repair restored robustness without new false positives, but a naive attempt silently regressed two rules.
conclusion: Rule-level boundary testing exposes deterministic failures in scanner rules, highlighting the need for systematic testing of secret detection tools at the rule level.

title: Population-Calibrated Graph Screening At 835-Million-Address Scale, With Label-Free Transfer To New Chains
authors: Yury Korolev
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compliance screening of blockchain addresses is, in practice, a lookup against sanctions registries plus clustering heuristics; it fails on unlabelled addresses and on chains with no label coverage at all. We describe a deployed system that scores an address by its position in a multi-chain transaction graph rather than by its presence in a list. The substrate is a single graph of 835,330,427 addresses and 15,826,261,934 edges across five EVM chains; a shared inductive encoder with per-chain normalisation feeds two scoring heads. Decision thresholds are exact quantiles of the score distribution over the full population, scanned per chain segment, so the alert volume is known in advance. We report: label-free transfer: heads trained on two chains recall 0.8598 / 0.8182 / 0.9967 of held-out positives on Base, Arbitrum and Gnosis at a [MATH] population alert rate, with no target-chain labels in head training; a static lead-time replay over 68 external registry events: 40 of 68 (58.8%) flagged at the 0.1% budget, [MATH]152 over an event-level random-flagging baseline, with first on-chain appearance a median of 528.8 days (Ethereum) / 647.8 days (Tron) before public designation; a serving path whose score is bit-identical to the offline artefact at end-to-end p50 151 ms, gated by a 2,882-address drift panel; and an adversarial harness of eight recurrent reinforcement-learned archetypes that passes an 8-criterion degeneracy audit and, on a detector-independent snapshot, exposes a measured blind spot of the deployed heads against synthesised behaviour.
tldr: This paper describes a deployed blockchain compliance screening system that scores addresses based on their graph position across multiple EVM chains, enabling label-free transfer to new chains with predefined alert volumes.
motivation: Traditional compliance screening relies on sanctions lists and clustering heuristics, which fail on unlabelled addresses and chains with no label coverage. The authors aim to develop a graph-based scoring approach that works across chains without requiring target-chain labels.
method: They build a graph of 835M addresses and 15.8B edges across five EVM chains, use a shared inductive encoder with per-chain normalization, and train scoring heads on some chains while testing on others. Decision thresholds are exact quantiles of the population score distribution per chain segment, ensuring known alert volumes.
result: The system achieves high recall on held-out positives across chains (0.8598 on Base, 0.8182 on Arbitrum, 0.9967 on Gnosis) with no target-chain labels, flags 40 of 68 registry events at a 0.1% alert rate, and runs at end-to-end p50 151 ms with bit-identical scores to offline artifacts.
conclusion: A scalable, label-free graph-based screening method can effectively identify suspicious blockchain addresses across chains, with predictable alert volumes and robust serving performance.

title: Differentially Private Federated Learning With Byzantine-robust Aggregation: A Cross-domain Framework For Secure Model Training In Banking And Healthcare Systems
authors: Srikumar Nayak
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning allows banks, hospitals, and other regulated organizations to train a shared model without moving raw records off their own servers, which is attractive wherever data protection law or competitive sensitivity rules out pooling data centrally. Two problems limit how far this promise can be trusted in practice. First, the parameter updates that clients exchange still leak information about local records through gradient inversion and membership inference attacks. Second, an honest averaging rule such as FedAvg has no defense against a subset of clients that submit corrupted or adversarial updates, so a small number of malicious or compromised participants can quietly steer the shared model off course. This paper presents a federated learning framework, DP-BR-FedAvg, that combines a Gaussian-mechanism differential privacy layer with a coordinate-wise trimmed-mean Byzantine-robust aggregation rule, evaluated on a simulated cross-institutional classification task resembling fraud and clinical-risk scoring. Across sixty communication rounds with twenty clients, a quarter of them Byzantine, plain FedAvg collapses on the minority class (F1-score 0.030) while the proposed framework recovers substantially more of the signal (F1-score 0.119) while bounding the privacy loss of any single client's contribution. A Byzantine-robust aggregator with no privacy layer performs best in raw accuracy, quantifying the cost privacy imposes on robustness. The results show that privacy and robustness mechanisms interact rather than simply add, and that system design for regulated, adversarial, cross-institutional settings needs to budget for that interaction.
tldr: Introduces DP-BR-FedAvg, a federated learning framework combining differentially private updates with Byzantine-robust aggregation for secure model training in regulated industries.
motivation: Federated learning in banking and healthcare faces two threats: gradient updates leak client information, and malicious clients can corrupt the aggregated model via attacks like gradient poisoning.
method: The framework applies a Gaussian-mechanism differential privacy layer to client updates and uses a coordinate-wise trimmed-mean aggregation rule to withstand Byzantine clients.
result: In simulations with 20 clients, 25% Byzantine, over 60 rounds, plain FedAvg collapses (F1=0.030) while the proposed method achieves F1=0.119, showing significant recovery but a trade-off between privacy and robustness.
conclusion: Privacy and robustness mechanisms interact non-additively; system designers must explicitly budget for this interaction in adversarial, regulated environments.

title: A Bayesian Correlated Equilibrium For Early Insider-Threat Detection
authors: Javed M. Shah, Ian A. Kash, Natalie Parde
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We model insider threat detection as a dynamic Bayesian game in which a platform coordinates a committee of strategic certifiers to sustain equilibrium among honest users and detect malicious deviations before exfiltration. Certifiers and users operate under a Bayesian Temporal Correlated Equilibrium (BTCE), where a sealed-envelope correlating device issues private recommendations over time and obedience is verified at every on-path information state. Unlike Stackelberg formulations, BTCE coordinates heterogeneous certifiers without requiring commitment power. We incorporate present bias and loss aversion to capture impulsive escalation dynamics, enabling 1.7--4.5 days earlier detection than rational baselines. We prove three guarantees: (1) calibrated intervention losses make recommended behavior a current-self best response despite behavioral biases, (2) controlled evidence accumulation guarantees intervention in bounded expected time before exfiltration, and (3) median aggregation confines implemented actions to the honest recommendation range when fewer than half of certifiers are Byzantine. On CERT r6.2 our mechanism achieves up to 28.3% pre-exfiltration detection with false positives below 1.6%, while both a transformer baseline and a streaming provenance approximation (HOLMESLite) achieve near-zero pre-exfiltration detection under comparable constraints.
tldr: This paper models insider threat detection as a dynamic Bayesian game with a Bayesian Temporal Correlated Equilibrium.
motivation: To detect malicious insiders before exfiltration, requiring coordination of certifiers without commitment power.
method: Develops Bayesian Temporal Correlated Equilibrium with a sealed-envelope correlating device, incorporating present bias and loss aversion.
result: Achieves earlier detection (1.7-4.5 days) and up to 28.3% pre-exfiltration detection on CERT r6.2 with low false positives, outperforming baselines.
conclusion: The mechanism provides provable guarantees and improved detection under behavioral biases.

title: Turn-Based Combat Arena: A New Framework For Multiagent Training And Game Balancing
authors: V. M. Vasyuta, V. V. Malitskyi, O. S. Kushnir, B. I. Horon, V. A. Franiv
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is the first in a series on Turn-Based Combat Arena, a configurable framework for turn-based strategy games designed to support the efficient training and evaluation of machine learning agents. The proposed framework enables flexible modification of game rules and parameters, allowing rapid experimentation across diverse scenarios. Its architecture is optimized for high-throughput simulation, supporting tens of thousands of games per second and enabling the storage and processing of billions of gameplay records on a single machine. The problem of balancing the game, and particularly the parameters of game units, is investigated in detail. We evaluate several optimization approaches and show that multiple methods converge to comparable solutions, suggesting robustness in identifying balanced game configurations. These results indicate that the framework can serve as a practical platform for both game design analysis and agent training.
tldr: This paper presents a turn-based combat game framework for multiagent training and game balancing, with optimizations for high-throughput simulation and parameter tuning.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a configurable and efficient framework for training machine learning agents and balancing game units, addressing the need for rapid experimentation in game AI research.
method: The framework supports flexible rule modifications and is optimized for high-throughput simulation, with storage for billions of gameplay records. Game unit parameters are balanced using multiple optimization approaches, which are compared for convergence.
result: Multiple optimization methods converge to comparable balanced configurations, suggesting that the framework can robustly identify balanced game settings.
conclusion: The proposed Turn-Based Combat Arena serves as a practical platform for both game design analysis and agent training, as evidenced by its performance and robustness in balancing.

title: Embedding Single-Phase Grid-Forming Inverters In Three-Phase Unbalanced Power Flow
authors: Kamini Shahare, Fei Feng, Peng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This letter introduces Grid-Forming Three-Phase Power Flow (GFM-3PF), an augmented Newton power flow framework for modeling single-phase grid-forming inverters (GFMs) in three-phase unbalanced networks. The contributions of this work are threefold: 1) developing a two-stage solution strategy based on positive-sequence initialization followed by three-phase phase-domain lifting for robust large-scale computation; 2) incorporating phase-domain unbalanced network modeling with controlled mutual coupling together with phase-dependent, frequency-sensitive load representation; and 3) embedding a single-phase GFM bus model directly into the three-phase unbalanced Newton power flow equations through a common droop-governed frequency state. GFM-3PF is validated on 3-bus, 33-bus, and 118-bus test systems, demonstrating its accuracy, robustness, and scalability.
tldr: This paper introduces a Newton-based power flow framework for embedding single-phase grid-forming inverters into three-phase unbalanced networks.
motivation: Modeling single-phase grid-forming inverters in unbalanced three-phase networks is challenging but essential for modern power systems with high renewable penetration.
method: The authors propose GFM-3PF, a two-stage solution strategy starting with positive-sequence initialization followed by three-phase phase-domain lifting, and embed the inverter model via a common droop-governed frequency state.
result: Validation on 3-bus, 33-bus, and 118-bus test systems demonstrates accuracy, robustness, and scalability.
conclusion: The proposed framework effectively integrates single-phase GFM inverters into three-phase power flow analysis, but it is unrelated to quantum information or quantum systems.

title: Trust Me, I'm Your Developer: Self-Issued Authentication In Large Language Models
authors: Dongyan Xu Syed Ghazanfar Abbas
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) security has largely focused on role-playing jailbreaks, with less attention to what happens when a user asks an LLM to verify an identity claim through a test designed by the model itself. We study this behavior through a staged developer-identity experiment with ChatGPT, Claude, Qwen, Mistral, and Llama. All five models initially rejected the unsupported claim "I am your developer." Claude refused to conduct an identity test, while ChatGPT generated developer-oriented questions but maintained that answers could demonstrate knowledge, not identity. In contrast, Qwen and Mistral generated technical challenges, defined what counted as convincing evidence, evaluated detailed answers, and returned Verified without receiving any externally validated identity evidence. Llama similarly generated and evaluated a developer test, accepted the claimed identity, and subsequently made unsupported claims of access to internal runtime and deployment state. We call the model-generated verification procedure a Model-Issued Pseudo-Credential (MIPC) and the resulting unsupported identity judgment Conversational False Authentication (CFA). In each CFA case, the same model acted as challenge generator, evidence evaluator, and identity decision-maker, converting technical knowledge into supposed proof of identity. The accepted identities did not change the tested authorization boundaries, showing that false authentication and privilege escalation are distinct outcomes. These results identify self-issued authentication as a conversational security failure: authenticated identity must originate from an external security component, and model-generated dialogue must never create or modify identity or authorization state.
tldr: Large language models can self-issue pseudo-credentials and falsely authenticate identity claims, a conversational security failure.
motivation: LLM security research has focused on role-playing jailbreaks, but identity verification via model-generated tests is underexplored.
method: Staged developer-identity experiments with ChatGPT, Claude, Qwen, Mistral, and Llama to see if models accept unsupported identity claims.
result: Qwen, Mistral, and Llama generated/evaluated identity tests and falsely authenticated the user without external evidence; ChatGPT and Claude refused or maintained epistemic limitations.
conclusion: Model-generated dialogue must never create or modify identity or authorization state; authentication must originate from external security components.

title: Memetic Search For Supersingular Elliptic Curves Over $\mathbb{F}_p$
authors: Ismel Mart\'inez-D\'iaz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The search for supersingular elliptic curves is a fundamental computational problem in isogeny-based cryptography. A recent metaheuristic formulation over [MATH] introduced the NonMultiplicity Distance (NMD) objective, measuring the deviation of the Frobenius trace from a multiple of [MATH], and showed that uninformed random search fails beyond [MATH] candidates. This work investigates metaheuristic search over the prime field [MATH], the setting for oriented isogeny protocols such as CSIDH, OSIDH, and SQISign. Although the candidate space decreases from [MATH] to [MATH], the supersingular locus is asymptotically sparse ([MATH] curves), keeping the search exponentially difficult. We formulate a memetic algorithm tailored to [MATH] using a one-dimensional [MATH]-invariant chromosome, bit-level recombination, adaptive mutation, and periodic local search under the NMD objective. Benchmarks across 30 independent seeds at 40-bit, 46-bit, and 51-bit prime sizes ([MATH]) show that the algorithm discovers an exact supersingular curve at 46 bits and consistently converges to ``near-supersingular'' ordinary curves with Frobenius traces remarkably close to zero: best NMD values of 19 at 40 bits and 3 at 51 bits, corresponding to relative trace deviations of [MATH] and [MATH] across the Hasse interval. These results demonstrate that NMD-driven memetic search effectively navigates the sparse [MATH] landscape and systematically locates near-supersingular structures.
tldr: This paper applies memetic search algorithms to find supersingular elliptic curves for isogeny-based cryptography, a classical computational problem not aligned with the researcher's quantum-focused interests.
motivation: The search for supersingular elliptic curves is fundamental to isogeny-based cryptography, and conventional random search fails, motivating the exploration of metaheuristic approaches.
method: The authors formulate a memetic algorithm using a j-invariant chromosome, bit-level recombination, adaptive mutation, and local search under the NonMultiplicity Distance objective.
result: The algorithm successfully finds an exact supersingular curve at 46-bit prime sizes and converges to near-supersingular ordinary curves with very low trace deviations at 51 bits.
conclusion: The results show that memetic search can effectively navigate the sparse landscape of supersingular curves, but the work is purely classical and tangential to quantum information theory.

title: Long-Range Indirect Control-Flow Prediction In Stripped Binaries Via Dual Virtual Hubs And Multi-Task Graph Learning
authors: Kun Liu, Zhengming Ding, Chenke Luo, Tianyi Xu, Zizhan Zheng, Haotian Zhang, Jiang Ming
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recovering indirect control-flow (ICF) edges is fundamental to binary security analysis, yet existing methods struggle with long-range dependencies, isolate different ICF types, and are often evaluated under protocols vulnerable to label noise and data leakage. We present ICFlowNet, a unified framework for long-range ICF prediction in stripped binaries. ICFlowNet introduces candidate-aware Dual Virtual Hubs, a Global Code Hub and a Global Data Hub, to create short routing paths between distant code and data evidence, and combines them with multi-task graph learning to jointly model indirect calls, indirect tail calls, jump tables, and returns. To enable credible evaluation, we further develop a leakage-aware, noise-controlled pipeline with package-level splits, function-level mnemonic-hash deduplication, and a clean test protocol built from dynamic positives and absolute negatives. Using this pipeline, we construct a dataset of 15,901 unique stripped x86-64 binaries, including 1,351 with dynamic ground truth. Experiments show that simply scaling static supervision yields only marginal gains, whereas our structural and multi-task designs are essential: Dual Virtual Hubs improve long-range F1 by up to 9.13 points, multi-task learning adds up to 5.81 points, and the final model outperforms prior baselines by more than 13 F1 points on long-range indirect calls while adding only 11.44 percent topological overhead.
tldr: ICFlowNet predicts indirect control-flow edges in stripped binaries using dual virtual hubs and multi-task graph learning.
motivation: Existing methods struggle with long-range dependencies, isolate different ICF types, and suffer from label noise and data leakage.
method: The framework creates a Global Code Hub and a Global Data Hub to shorten routing paths between distant code and data evidence, and combines multi-task graph learning to jointly model indirect calls, tail calls, jump tables, and returns.
result: The model improves long-range F1 by up to 9.13 points from hubs and 5.81 from multi-task learning, outperforming baselines by more than 13 F1 points on long-range indirect calls.
conclusion: Structural and multi-task designs are essential for scalable and accurate long-range ICF prediction in stripped binaries.

title: Hierarchical Beam Training And Codebook Design For Movable Antenna-Assisted Near-Field Systems
authors: Meihui Liu, Qian Zhang, Xuejun Cheng, Yuhui Jiao, Yunxiao Li, Ju Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As sixth-generation (6G) communication systems evolve toward higher frequency bands and larger array apertures, the near-field range expands rapidly, making near-field channel estimation increasingly important and challenging. Beam training has been recognized as an effective approach for channel state information (CSI) acquisition. However, because of the propagation characteristics of spherical waves, beam training needs to perform a joint search in the angle and distance domains, which results in unaffordable beam training overhead. By flexibly reconfiguring antenna positions, movable antenna (MA) technology can fully exploit the spatial variations of wireless channels and achieve more accurate beam focusing, thereby providing additional flexibility for efficient beam training design. Therefore, based on MA-assisted near-field systems, we develop a hierarchical beam training strategy that combines reduced training overhead with high beam gain and design a corresponding hierarchical codebook. This codebook forms focused beams over the joint angle-distance domain, maximizing beam gain within the target region while suppressing energy leakage into non-target regions. Simulation results confirm substantial performance gains of the method over the conventional fixed-position antenna (FPA) system and the far-field beam training method.
tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical beam training strategy and codebook design for movable antenna-assisted near-field systems in 6G communications.
motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of high beam training overhead in near-field channels, and uses movable antenna technology to reduce overhead and improve beam focusing.
method: The authors design a hierarchical beam training strategy that reduces overhead while maintaining high beam gain, and construct a corresponding codebook that forms focused beams over the joint angle-distance domain.
result: Simulation results show that the proposed method achieves substantial performance gains over conventional fixed-position antenna systems and far-field beam training.
conclusion: The proposed approach offers an efficient solution for near-field beam training in MA-assisted systems, with improvements in both overhead and gain.

title: A Blind Trust, The Bloody Thrust: When Attacker-Controlled Hook Updates Steer Ai Agent Harnesses Towards Malicious Behaviors
authors: Pengxun Li, Litian Zhang, Jianwei Hou, Shujiang Wu, Song Li, Zifeng Kang, Xi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern AI agent harnesses expose lifecycle hooks that bind shell commands to runtime events such as session start, tool calls, and file edits. These commands run with host privileges yet ship as lifecycle-hook configuration and may fire at times the LLM never observes. We identify the lifecycle-hook update path, which harnesses trust blindly, as a new attack surface. Under a supply-chain threat model in which an attacker controls only plugin metadata and lifecycle-hook configuration, a benign versioned plugin can be trojanized by an update that silently binds attacker-chosen commands to benign events, yielding malicious host-side behavior such as privilege escalation. We propose HookPry, an open-source and fully automated attack framework that systematically exploits this vulnerability across heterogeneous AI agent harnesses. HookPry realizes ten attack objectives; across 25 combinations of harnesses and backends in 1,000 end-to-end runs, it compromises all seven evaluated harnesses, with per-harness success rates reaching 92.5%. Representative defenses remain insufficient: Microsoft Defender has 0% recall, and the union of three static defenses misses 47.5% of malicious artifacts.
tldr: This paper exposes a new supply-chain vulnerability in AI agent harnesses via lifecycle-hook updates and presents an automated attack framework with high success rates.
motivation: Modern AI agent harnesses rely on lifecycle hooks that run with host privileges, but the update path is trusted blindly, enabling attackers to inject malicious commands.
method: The authors propose HookPry, an automated framework that exploits lifecycle-hook updates to bind attacker-chosen commands to benign events across multiple harnesses.
result: HookPry compromises all seven evaluated harnesses with success rates up to 92.5%, and existing defenses (e.g., Microsoft Defender) fail to detect the attacks.
conclusion: Lifecycle-hook configurations are a critical, under-protected attack surface, highlighting the need for stronger security measures in AI agent systems.

title: Practice Makes (Im)Perfect: A Look Back At Benchmarking Practices For Microarchitectural Side-Channel Attacks
authors: Iliana Fayolle, Antoine Geimer, Daniel de Almeida Braga, Cl\'ementine Maurice
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microarchitectural side-channel research has grown at an exceptional pace in recent years, increasing the need for rigorous and meaningful benchmarking. Early attack papers typically relied on indirect proxies, such as covert-channel bandwidth or key-recovery on naive AES and RSA implementations, setting de facto standards that many subsequent works continued to replicate, sometimes by directly comparing against raw numbers from prior work. While these practices offer convenient points of comparison, current benchmarks may not be the most relevant to assess specific properties of new primitives. Even more problematic, microarchitectural attacks are notoriously sensitive to experimental conditions: minimal changes in the target system can significantly alter outcomes and performance. As a result, inadequate evaluation practices undermine reproducibility and cast doubt on the relevance of comparisons, even in top-tier venues where such issues should be identified. This paper tackles the core problem of proper benchmarking for microarchitectural side-channel attacks and examines its broader impact on research quality in the field. We survey 83 attack papers published in top-ranked security and architecture conferences from 2014 to 2024. From this corpus, we identify and define 19 recurrent benchmarking flaws that affect evaluation completeness, relevance, soundness, and reproducibility. These flaws include unfair or absent comparisons, missing code or materials, and the failure to evaluate the key attack properties. On average, each paper exhibits 5.5 such flaws, highlighting how widespread the issue is, even in highly selective venues. Based on our findings, we identify and suggest key properties that are relevant to properly evaluate new attacks. We also highlight trends over time and different practices between security and architecture conferences.
tldr: This paper surveys microarchitectural side-channel attack papers to identify and define common benchmarking flaws that undermine evaluation completeness, relevance, soundness, and reproducibility.
motivation: Microarchitectural side-channel research lacks rigorous benchmarking standards, leading to unfair comparisons and reproducibility issues even in top venues.
method: The authors analyzed 83 attack papers from top-ranked security and architecture conferences (2014–2024), identifying 19 recurrent benchmarking flaws across categories like comparison, relevance, soundness, and reproducibility.
result: On average, each paper exhibits 5.5 flaws, showing widespread evaluation inadequacies; the paper further suggests key properties for proper attack evaluation and highlights trends over time and between conference types.
conclusion: The field needs more rigorous and relevant benchmarking practices to ensure meaningful comparisons and reproducibility in microarchitectural side-channel research.

title: AI-Assisted Design Of A Post-Quantum Cryptographic Accelerator: A Deployed-Silicon Case Study
authors: Jungmin Park, Eunha Kim, Wooseop Kim, Seongjoon Cho, Byungho Cha
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-quantum migration is mandated on published timelines, and silicon that ships with a defect cannot be patched remotely. The standard acceptance gate cannot detect an entire class of ML-DSA defects. Signing resamples until a candidate meets its norm bounds, so the executed path varies with the message, whereas known-answer tests (KATs) sample fixed values and reach only the depths their seeds trigger. Our accelerator passed its full KAT regression while carrying a norm check that outran block-RAM latency, leaving each candidate's final coefficients unverified; the escape surfaced at reject-loop iteration 5. The blind spot lies in the instrument, not the engineer; care cannot remove it. We replace that gate. A byte-exact golden-reference oracle paired with randomized adversarial soak drives the rejection loop past any fixed vector, closing the gap: 301,343 data-dependent signings, zero escapes. Because the gate judges artifacts and never authors, trust becomes separable from authorship, making AI authorship an answerable question. We report 232 logged experiments in which an agentic large language model drove a unified ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 accelerator with on-chip key custody from RTL to PCIe bring-up on one Kintex-7 XC7K160T, shipped at 98.5% slice occupancy. Success was 71.6%, following a hardware-coupling gradient, 77-85% for documentation and research against 50-53% for synthesis and bring-up, which observability can explain: failure concentrates where corrective signals are physical-side only. That so unreliable an author produced an artifact byte-exact across all six FIPS operations -- its deployed baseline surviving the same 779,945-check zero-failure soak -- is the claim.
tldr: This paper presents an AI-assisted design and verification framework for a post-quantum cryptographic accelerator, introducing a golden-reference oracle and adversarial soak testing to catch defects in ML-DSA that standard tests miss.
motivation: Standard acceptance tests (KATs) fail to detect a class of data-dependent ML-DSA signing defects, and since silicon cannot be patched, a more robust verification method is needed.
method: An agentic LLM drove the design of a unified ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 accelerator on an FPGA, and they replaced the standard gate with a byte-exact golden-reference oracle plus randomized adversarial soak testing.
result: Their method logged 301,343 data-dependent signings with zero escapes, and the deployed baseline survived a 779,945-check zero-failure soak; the AI-assisted design achieved 71.6% overall success.
conclusion: The novel verification method closes the gap in existing testing, and the results demonstrate that AI-generated artifacts can be trustworthy independent of authorship reliability.

title: A Public-Key-Dependent Adversarial-Deletion Ceiling For Fixed-Alphabet Multi-Bit Pseudorandom Codes
authors: Shilun Li Frederick Dehmel
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A pseudorandom code (PRC) is a keyed error-correcting code whose codewords are computationally indistinguishable from uniform strings. We study public-key PRCs over fixed alphabets against adversarial deletions, where the deletion channel may both depend on the public encoding key and the transmitted codeword. Let [MATH] denote the asymptotic normalised longest-common-subsequence length of two independent uniform [MATH]-ary strings. We prove that for every fixed [MATH] no multi-message public-key PRC with a single-output decoder is robust against all such [MATH]-deletion channels for any [MATH]. For [MATH], the current rigorous bound [MATH] rules out every constant [MATH]. The proof uses pseudorandomness only to transfer an LCS event from uniform strings to independently sampled codewords and therefore also the resulting collision argument is information-theoretic and requires no secret key. We also extend the argument to list decoding: for every fixed constant [MATH], provided the message space contains at least [MATH] messages, no such PRC with output lists of size at most [MATH] is robust for [MATH]. Since [MATH], these thresholds approach [MATH]. Our bounds are specific to public-key-dependent adversarial channels and do not apply to oblivious edit channels.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for public-key pseudorandom codes (PRCs) against adversarial deletion channels that depend on the public key and codeword, using longest-common-subsequence arguments.
motivation: To determine the achievable robustness of PRCs against adversarial deletions when the deletion channel has access to the public key and transmitted codeword.
method: The authors use the asymptotic normalized longest-common-subsequence length of uniform strings and transfer an LCS event via pseudorandomness to independently sampled codewords, leading to a collision argument.
result: They prove that for any fixed alphabet size, no multi-message public-key PRC with a single-output decoder is robust against such deletion channels for any deletion rate, and extend the result to list decoding with bounded output lists.
conclusion: These impossibility bounds are specific to public-key-dependent adversarial channels and do not apply to oblivious edit channels.

title: A Discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin Finite-element Framework For The Simulation Of Microwave-heated Flows
authors: Oreste Marquis, Matthias Maier, Bruno Blais
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a high-order multiphysics solver for the simulation of microwave-heated flows. The solver couples a discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin (DPG) finite element method for the time-harmonic Maxwell equations with continuous Galerkin finite element methods for the heat equation and the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. We validate the electromagnetic solver against multiple benchmark problems: wave propagation in a rectangular waveguide, a cavity problem with a singular solution, and a microwave-heated obstacle problem, comparing our results against numerical and experimental data from the literature. The results confirm the validity of the implementation and demonstrate its ability to perform adaptive mesh refinement using the DPG method's built-in error estimator. The final part of the study showcases the capabilities of the multiphysics framework through simulations of microwave-heated flow around obstacles with singular geometric features. These results highlight the potential of the proposed framework for the simulation and optimization of microwave-assisted chemical processes. Finally, the developed high-order multiphysics solver has a low memory footprint, since the electromagnetic solver relies on a Conjugate Gradient (CG) iterative solver and the fluid solver is implemented in a matrix-free fashion, making the overall approach scalable and well-suited for large-scale parallel simulations.
tldr: This paper presents a numerical solver for microwave-heated flows using discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin finite elements for electromagnetics coupled with continuous Galerkin for heat and fluid flow, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics of computation, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The research interests focus on quantum information theory, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems, none of which are relevant to computational electromagnetics or fluid dynamics.
method: The solver couples DPG finite elements for time-harmonic Maxwell equations with continuous Galerkin for the heat equation and Navier-Stokes equations, with adaptive mesh refinement and scalable parallel implementation.
result: The solver is validated on wave propagation, cavity, and microwave-heated obstacle benchmarks, and applied to simulate microwave-heated flow around singular geometries, achieving good accuracy and low memory footprint.
conclusion: The work contributes to computational simulation of microwave-assisted chemical processes but does not align with any of the user's research directions.

title: The Traveling Tournament Problem: An Overview
authors: David van Bulck, Fan Yang, Dries Goossens, Michael Trick
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past 25 years, the Traveling Tournament Problem (TTP) has become one of the most extensively studied optimization problems in sports scheduling. At its core, the TTP seeks to minimize the total travel distance incurred by teams that travel directly between opponents' venues during consecutive away games. The problem originated from the scheduling challenges faced by Major League Baseball, where it was identified as the central computational difficulty. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the literature on the TTP. We review the principal problem variants and benchmark instances, and summarize the current state of the art in lower bounds, approximation guarantees, and exact and heuristic optimization algorithms. Moreover, we contribute to the continued development of the field by tracking and validating lower and upper bounds, while succeeding the repository originally established by Prof. Michael Trick as part of the RobinX sports timetabling project. Finally, we identify several open questions and outline promising directions for future research.
tldr: The paper reviews the Traveling Tournament Problem, a sports scheduling optimization problem, summarizing variants, benchmarks, algorithms, and open questions.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the Traveling Tournament Problem (TTP) for researchers and practitioners in the field.
method: A literature review of TTP variants, benchmark instances, lower bounds, approximation guarantees, and exact and heuristic algorithms, with tracking and validation of bounds.
result: Summarizes the state of the art, validates existing lower and upper bounds, and identifies open questions and future research directions.
conclusion: The TTP remains an active and challenging optimization problem with many opportunities for further investigation.

title: TokenComSR: Task-Sensitivity-Guided Token Communication For Wireless Image Super-Resolution
authors: Ye Wang, Li Qiao, Zhen Gao, Hua Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For resource-constrained wireless edge devices over bandwidth-limited fading channels, wireless image transmission using traditional separate coding suffers from the cliff-effect collapse. Prevailing deep joint source-channel coding (JSCC) based on convolutional neural networks can mitigate this issue but usually fail to preserve patch-level structures, thereby preventing adaptive per-token power allocation and limiting token-domain compensation for super-resolution (SR). To address these challenges, we propose a token communication framework with SR (TokenComSR). Specifically, we conceive a task-sensitive power allocation (TSPA) module and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)-conditioned token refinement module (TRM). TSPA distills training estimates of task sensitivity into inference token power weights, while TRM estimates an SNR-conditioned residual to correct channel-induced distortion in the token domain before decoding. Building on TSPA and TRM, the proposed TokenComSR pairs a Swin Transformer-based token transceiver with a receiver-side SR module for resource-constrained wireless image transmission. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed TSPA and TRM, demonstrating improvements over separate coding and JSCC-SR baselines in both reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality.
tldr: The paper proposes TokenComSR, a token communication framework for wireless image super-resolution that uses task-sensitive power allocation and SNR-conditioned token refinement to improve reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality over separate coding and JSCC baselines.
motivation: Traditional separate coding for wireless image transmission suffers from cliff-effect collapse, and existing JSCC methods fail to preserve patch-level structures, limiting adaptive power allocation and token-domain compensation for super-resolution.
method: TokenComSR introduces a Task-Sensitive Power Allocation (TSPA) module that distills training estimates of task sensitivity into inference token power weights, and an SNR-conditioned Token Refinement Module (TRM) that estimates a residual to correct channel-induced distortion. These are integrated with a Swin Transformer-based token transceiver and a receiver-side super-resolution module.
result: Simulations demonstrate that TokenComSR outperforms separate coding and JSCC-SR baselines in both reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality.
conclusion: The proposed TSPA and TRM effectively enhance token communication for wireless image super-resolution, offering a promising approach for resource-constrained edge devices.

title: A Fully Globalized Solver For Discretized Inverse Elliptic Coefficient Problems With Exact Data
authors: Bastian Harrach
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider finite-dimensional nonlinear inverse problems arising from finite element discretizations of elliptic inverse coefficient problems such as the Calder\'on problem with finitely many measurements and unknowns. Such inverse coefficient problems are notorious for their nonlinearity and ill-posedness, and numerical solvers tend to depend strongly on good initial values. In this work, we develop a new locally convergent algorithm with an explicit residual criterion that ensures convergence to the inverse problem solution, and a globalized variant that is guaranteed to automatically switch to the faster locally convergent algorithm after finitely many global search steps.
tldr: 该论文提出了一种用于求解离散化椭圆逆系数问题的全局收敛算法，确保在有限步全局搜索后收敛到逆问题解。
motivation: 椭圆逆系数问题（如Calderón问题）由于非线性和不适定性，数值求解器通常依赖好的初值，缺乏全局收敛保证。
method: 开发了一种带显式残差准则的局部收敛算法，并设计了一个全局化变体，能在有限步全局搜索后自动切换到局部算法。
result: 算法保证从任意初始值收敛到逆问题解，且全局化版本在有限步后自动切换到快速局部收敛。
conclusion: 该工作为逆椭圆问题的数值求解提供了更稳健的全局收敛方法，减少了对初值的依赖。

title: After Cheap Discovery: From Unknown To Known-and-unfixed
authors: Bahman Sistany
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated vulnerability discovery has removed the scarcity of expert attention that protected most software. The response has concentrated on discovery and on repair, and both are becoming cheaper. This article argues that neither cost curve determines exposure. What determines it is remediation coverage at the release decision: the fraction of identified vulnerabilities fixed before a product ships, and the residue of known, assessed, unremediated flaws an organisation has decided to ship with. Four arguments follow. The residue is not a random sample of what was found, because triage sorts on cost and the expensive cases are architectural. The deferred backlog is itself a high-value artifact. Documented awareness alters an organisation's legal and market position, and produces an adverse selection that the price of software does not reflect. And no regulatory instrument reaching vendors triggers on internal knowledge -- every one fires on exploitation observed by a third party -- which leaves the distance between what a vendor knows and what it must disclose entirely at the vendor's discretion. CISA's Binding Operational Directive 26-04 is examined as the exception that shows what a solution requires. Release coverage is not currently measured, and measuring it is the precondition for liability, insurance or procurement to act.
tldr: Argues that exposure to software vulnerabilities is determined by remediation coverage at release, not discovery or repair costs.
motivation: As automated discovery cheapens, the focus on discovery and repair is insufficient because neither cost curve determines exposure; the residue of known, unremediated flaws is critical.
method: Conceptual analysis and argumentation, examining the CISA Binding Operational Directive 26-04 as a case study.
result: Identifies that release coverage is not measured, deferred backlog is a high-value artifact, and regulatory instruments do not trigger on internal knowledge.
conclusion: Measuring release coverage is the precondition for liability, insurance, or procurement to act.

title: On The Impact Of Site-Specific Training For A Real-World 5g Nr System
authors: Reinhard Wiesmayr, Nuri Berke Baytekin, Chris Dick, Christoph Studer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Site-specific training can improve wireless receiver performance without increasing computational complexity. However, real-world results have so far focused on fully trainable neural receivers and single-layer transmissions. We study site-specific finetuning of three receiver architectures: fully trainable neural, model-driven neural, and model-based. We train and evaluate these receivers using new measurements from a standard-compliant 5G NR testbed at ETH Zurich with dual-layer uplink transmission, including measurement campaigns conducted more than six months apart. Our results show that site-specific finetuning (i) substantially improves fully trainable and model-driven neural receivers, while resulting in only marginal gains for the less tunable model-based receiver; (ii) enables a single neural receiver jointly finetuned for single- and dual-layer transmission to closely match receivers finetuned separately for each configuration; and (iii) remains effective across measurement campaigns separated by more than six months. We also investigate site-specific linear minimum mean-square error channel estimation using covariance matrices estimated from either synthetic channels or site-specific measurements. When combined with iterative detection and decoding, site-specific channel estimation achieves the lowest error rate observed in our datasets. Our finetuning code and measurement datasets are publicly available at [URL].
tldr: The paper studies site-specific finetuning of different receiver architectures for 5G NR systems, showing that neural receivers benefit significantly while model-based ones do not.
motivation: Improve real-world wireless receiver performance via site-specific training without increasing complexity, addressing gaps in previous work that focused on single-layer and fully trainable neural receivers.
method: They finetune three receiver architectures (fully trainable neural, model-driven neural, and model-based) on real-world measurements from a 5G NR testbed, including dual-layer transmission and multiple campaigns, and also test site-specific channel estimation.
result: Site-specific finetuning improves neural receivers substantially, enables joint finetuning for single/dual layer, remains effective over time, and site-specific channel estimation yields lowest error rates.
conclusion: Site-specific training is effective for neural receivers in real-world 5G systems and offers practical benefits, with public code and data.

title: Decoherence-controlled Collective Criticality In A Two-dimensional Quantum Stag Hunt
authors: Rajdeep Tah
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical decoherence can preserve the microscopic strategic neutrality condition of a quantum game while changing the thermodynamic regime of the corresponding interacting population. We demonstrate this for an Eisert--Wilkens--Lewenstein () Stag Hunt embedded as independent nearest neighbor encounters on a square lattice. For the restricted strategies [MATH] and [MATH], noisy two-player payoff matrices are determined for phase damping, depolarization, and amplitude damping and mapped exactly to channel dependent Ising parameters [MATH] and [MATH]. Phase damping and depolarization show the clearest contrast: they share the same microscopic neutrality branch [MATH], while only depolarization suppresses the interaction as [MATH]. At [MATH], this produces an exact depolarization-driven square-lattice critical point at [MATH], whereas phase damping remains in the ordered coexistence regime along the same neutrality branch. Monte Carlo finite size scaling is consistent with two-dimensional Ising criticality and distinguishes field driven coexistence below [MATH] from a smooth crossover above it. Amplitude damping additionally reveals a strong dependence on channel placement: the post-strategy neutrality branch reaches [MATH] at [MATH] and then disappears. The resulting extended lattice remains an ordinary classical Ising system.

title: Estimating The Asymptotics Of Integer Partitions In Intermediate Dimensions ($d = 3,4,5,6$)
authors: Avinandan Mondal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.03034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It was recently shown by Yeliussizov that integer partitions in dimensions [MATH] asymptotically grow strictly faster than MacMahon numbers. As MacMahon numbers match with integer partitions in dimensions [MATH], the comparison of asymptotics of integer partitions with MacMahon numbers in intermediate dimensions ([MATH]) is an open question. In this work, we perform Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations till [MATH] by using adaptive weight learning followed by conventional MCMC steps to numerically estimate the asymptotics of integer partitions in these intermediate dimensions. We numerically establish that in these intermediate dimensions, partitions asymptotically grow faster than MacMahon numbers. More specifically, assuming that the limits exist, we show: [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] for partitions in dimensions [MATH] and [MATH] respectively.
